title: RetryExhausted log lines include full job arguments (customer PII in our logs)
body:
When a job is dead-lettered, the worker logs its full arguments. Our reminder jobs take contact
details, so personal data ends up in a log platform that has much wider access and longer
retention than our database. From staging this morning:

```text
2025-10-15T08:12:44Z ERROR orbit.worker  [ORB-1301] RetryExhausted: job 01J9X8K2RD send_sms_reminder failed 3/3 attempts; moved to DLQ args={"customer_email": "maria.gomez@example.com", "phone": "+1-555-0187", "address": "48 Sample Lane, Apt 3, Springfield", "appointment": "2025-10-16T09:30"}
2025-10-15T08:12:51Z ERROR orbit.worker  [ORB-1301] RetryExhausted: job 01J9X8K3ZB send_sms_reminder failed 3/3 attempts; moved to DLQ args={"customer_email": "alex.sample@example.com", "phone": "+1-555-0122", "address": "9 Placeholder Road, Springfield", "appointment": "2025-10-16T11:00"}
```

For GDPR purposes we need to keep this out of logs. Could argument values be left out (or made
opt-in)? The DLQ already stores the arguments for replay, so the log doesn't need them.
author: ember-ci

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Agreed. Logging argument values was meant as a debugging aid, but it's the wrong default. The
change: `RetryExhausted` lines will include the job ID, function, attempts and the last error,
but no argument values. The arguments stay available in the DLQ (`orbit dlq list`, the
dashboard), which you can restrict access to.

Separately, since issues are public: please confirm these are seed data. If not, edit them out
of the post.

Longer term, passing a `customer_id` instead of contact details keeps PII out of the broker too.
`security` has a section on what not to put in job arguments, and `dead-letter-queue` describes
what the DLQ keeps.

comments.author: ember-ci
comments.body: Yes, staging seed data, not real customers. Thanks for the quick turnaround.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Merged for 2.9.0. Closing.

title: Kubernetes docs: explain terminationGracePeriodSeconds for long jobs
body:
Every rolling deploy re-runs some of our jobs. It took us a while to work out why: Kubernetes'
default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is 30, our jobs take up to 10 minutes, so the worker gets
SIGTERM, starts draining, and is SIGKILLed 30 seconds later. The jobs then come back after the
lease expires.

The Kubernetes deployment page should say this prominently, with an example.
author: pebble-queue

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Thanks, it's one of the most common surprises. `deployment-kubernetes` now has a "Graceful
shutdown" section: set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to at least your longest expected job,
what the worker does on SIGTERM, and why a SIGKILL leads to redelivery. It links to
`troubleshooting-duplicates`. Closing.

title: 3.0 preview: migrate-config fails with ORB-1801 but doesn't say which key
body:
Testing the 3.0 preview from `main`. Our `orbit.ini` uses standard ConfigParser interpolation:

```ini
[DEFAULT]
redis_host = redis.internal.example.com

[orbit]
broker_url = redis://%(redis_host)s:6379/0
concurrency = 8
lease = 900
```

`orbit migrate-config` refuses it, without saying what it didn't like:

```text
$ orbit migrate-config orbit.ini
error: [ORB-1801] ConfigMigrationError: could not convert orbit.ini
```

Removing the interpolation makes it work. Two requests: support (or at least detect) interpolation,
and name the key in the error.
author: lumen-forge

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Thanks for trying the converter early. The converter reads `orbit.ini` without interpolation on
purpose, so `%(redis_host)s` reaches the URL parser literally and fails there. We'd rather not
resolve interpolation silently: the resolved values would then be frozen into `orbit.toml` in a
way that's easy to miss in review.

So the plan is: interpolation stays unsupported and is documented in the migration guide (convert
those keys by hand), and ORB-1801 should name the key it couldn't convert. Keeping this open
for the second part.

comments.author: lumen-forge
comments.body: Makes sense. Naming the key is the important bit.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
3.0.3 is out and `ConfigMigrationError` (ORB-1801) now names the `orbit.ini` key it couldn't
convert. Interpolation is listed as unsupported in `migrating-2-to-3`. Closing.

title: BrokerRateLimited on FIFO queue after adding more workers
body:
We doubled our worker count on a `.fifo` queue to get through a backlog, and throughput went
*down*. Logs:

```text
2025-10-22T12:58:10Z WARN  orbit.broker.sqs [ORB-1901] BrokerRateLimited: ReceiveMessage throttled on billing-default.fifo (attempt 2/5, retrying in 0.4s)
2025-10-22T12:58:11Z WARN  orbit.broker.sqs [ORB-1901] BrokerRateLimited: ReceiveMessage throttled on billing-default.fifo (attempt 3/5, retrying in 0.8s)
```

Is there a recommended number of workers per FIFO queue?
author: basalt-bee

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
There's no magic number, but more workers on one FIFO queue usually means more throttling, as you
saw. It's the same issue as #9: FIFO quotas are much lower than standard queues, and all jobs of
one function share a `MessageGroupId`, so extra workers just compete for the same group. See #9
for the options, and the FIFO section of `broker-sqs`. Closing as a duplicate of #9.

title: Nightly job ran twice on the DST change in Europe (ORB-1402)
body:
Our workers run with `TZ=Europe/Berlin`. The nightly book-closing job is scheduled with:

```python
app.schedule(close_books, cron="30 2 * * *")
```

On Sunday 26 October the clocks went back from 03:00 CEST to 02:00 CET, so 02:30 happened twice,
and the job ran twice. The second run posted duplicate ledger entries that finance had to
reverse by hand. Scheduler log (UTC timestamps):

```text
2025-10-26T00:30:00Z INFO  orbit.scheduler w-1 enqueued close_books (cron "30 2 * * *")
2025-10-26T01:30:00Z WARN  orbit.scheduler w-1 [ORB-1402] ScheduleDrift: close_books due 2025-10-26T02:30:00+02:00 fired 2025-10-26T02:30:00+01:00 (local time repeated by DST transition)
2025-10-26T01:30:00Z INFO  orbit.scheduler w-1 enqueued close_books (cron "30 2 * * *")
```

Orbit clearly *knows* it's a repeated local time, since it logs ORB-1402, and fires anyway. In
March I suspect the opposite happens (the run is skipped or late). I'd expect one run per
calendar day.
author: quartz-moth

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Sorry about the finance cleanup. This is a known, long-standing limitation rather than a new
regression. Cron expressions are evaluated in the **local time zone of the worker holding the
scheduler lock**, and Orbit has no per-schedule time zone. In a zone with DST, a fall-back night
repeats an hour (so a run can fire twice) and a spring-forward night skips one (so a run fires
late). ORB-1402 is logged in both cases. It's a warning, not a guard.

The supported fix:

1. Run every worker in **UTC** (`TZ=UTC`) and write the cron expression in UTC. `30 0 * * *` is
   02:30 CEST in summer and 01:30 CET in winter. If the business rule really is "02:30 Berlin
   time", schedule hourly and let the job decide whether it's time to act.
2. Make `close_books` idempotent per accounting day, so a second run is a no-op.

Details in `scheduling-cron` (Time zones and DST) and `faq`. Keeping this open as the tracking
issue for DST behaviour.

comments.author: quartz-moth
comments.body:
Moved the workers to UTC and added a per-day guard to the job. A "fire at most once per local
calendar day" mode would still be nice.

title: Rate limit a job type (max N runs per minute)
body:
A partner API we call allows 100 requests per minute per account. We'd love to declare that on the
job and have Orbit spread the work:

```python
@app.job(retries=5, backoff="exponential", rate_limit="100/m")
def push_to_partner(record_id: str): ...
```

Today we get bursts of 429s whenever a backlog builds up, and retries with backoff eventually
get through, but it's noisy and slow.
author: orchid-stack

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Understood. A cluster-wide rate limit needs shared state on the broker and has to behave the same
on all three brokers, so it isn't something we can add quickly. Patterns that work today:

- Put the job on its **own queue** with a dedicated worker and a fixed `--concurrency`. That caps
  how many calls run at once, which is often enough to stay under a per-minute limit.
- Treat 429 as a normal failure and let `retries` + exponential backoff spread the load. See
  `retries-and-backoff`.
- If you need a hard per-minute limit, use a token bucket in your own Redis inside the job.

Keeping this open as a feature request.

title: US DST change: 01:15 payroll export ran twice, ORB-1402 in logs
body:
Workers run with `TZ=America/Chicago`. We schedule a payroll export at 01:15:

```python
app.schedule(export_payroll, cron="15 1 * * *")
```

Yesterday (2 November) clocks fell back at 02:00, so 01:15 happened twice and the export ran
twice. The payroll provider rejected the second file, luckily.

```text
2025-11-02T06:15:00Z INFO  orbit.scheduler w-3 enqueued export_payroll (cron "15 1 * * *")
2025-11-02T07:15:00Z WARN  orbit.scheduler w-3 [ORB-1402] ScheduleDrift: export_payroll due 2025-11-02T01:15:00-05:00 fired 2025-11-02T01:15:00-06:00 (local time repeated by DST transition)
2025-11-02T07:15:00Z INFO  orbit.scheduler w-3 enqueued export_payroll (cron "15 1 * * *")
```
author: tin-lantern

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Same root cause as #59, which hit Europe a week earlier. Cron expressions are evaluated in the
local time zone of the lock-holding worker, so a repeated local hour fires twice. ORB-1402 is a
warning, not a guard.

Fix: run workers in UTC and write the expression in UTC, and make the export idempotent per pay
date. See `scheduling-cron`. Closing as a duplicate of #59. Please follow that issue for any
changes.

title: cron jobs off by an hour since sunday
body: all our scheduled jobs run one hour early since sunday. nothing changed on our side. orbit bug?
author: orchid-stack

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Sunday was the end of daylight saving time in the US, so this is almost certainly DST rather than
a change in Orbit. Two common setups produce exactly "one hour early since Sunday":

- workers run in **UTC**, and the cron expressions were written to match local *summer* time.
  The UTC times didn't move, but local time did;
- workers run in a local zone and the job compares against a UTC clock somewhere.

Which time zone do your workers run in (`TZ`), and what's one of the cron expressions? See #59
and the Time zones and DST section of `scheduling-cron`.

comments.author: orchid-stack
comments.body:
we run in UTC and wrote the crons for summer time, so yeah that's it. we'll just change them twice
a year i guess

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
That's the trade-off with UTC schedules, as documented. If it matters, schedule hourly and let the
job decide based on local time. Closing as a duplicate of #59.

title: Docker Compose में worker शुरू करते ही ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError
body:
नमस्ते, मैं Orbit को Docker Compose में चला रहा हूँ। मेरे laptop पर सब ठीक चलता है, लेकिन
container में worker शुरू करते ही यह error आता है:

```text
2025-11-06T06:41:09Z ERROR orbit.broker  [ORB-1001] BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to localhost:6379. Connection refused.
2025-11-06T06:41:11Z WARN  orbit.broker  retrying broker connection in 2.0s (attempt 2)
2025-11-06T06:41:15Z WARN  orbit.broker  retrying broker connection in 4.0s (attempt 3)
```

मेरी `docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7
  worker:
    build: .
    command: orbit worker --queues default
    environment:
      ORBIT_BROKER_URL: "redis://localhost:6379/0"
```

Redis container चल रहा है (`docker compose ps` में दिखता है)। क्या मुझे कोई port खोलना पड़ेगा?
मैं Orbit 2.8.0 और Python 3.11.9 इस्तेमाल कर रहा हूँ।

कृपया मदद करें।
author: monsoon-dev

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Namaste! Inside a container, `localhost` means *that container*, not your laptop and not the
`redis` container. Compose gives every service a hostname equal to its service name, so use:

```yaml
    environment:
      ORBIT_BROKER_URL: "redis://redis:6379/0"
    depends_on:
      - redis
```

No ports need to be published for container-to-container traffic. `ports:` is only for reaching
Redis from your host. See `deployment-docker`, and `troubleshooting-broker` for reading ORB-1001
messages.

(संक्षेप में: `localhost` की जगह service का नाम `redis` लिखें।)

comments.author: monsoon-dev
comments.body: धन्यवाद! `redis://redis:6379/0` से काम हो गया।

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Glad it works. Closing.

title: Windows container: `docker stop` doesn't drain the worker
body:
We run workers in Windows containers on Windows Server. On `docker stop`, the worker logs nothing,
keeps working, and Docker kills it after the timeout. The jobs that were running get picked up
again later by another worker, so some side effects happen twice.

On Linux containers the same image (well, the Linux build of it) drains cleanly on `docker stop`.
author: sundial-ops

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
This is the known Windows shutdown problem tracked in #16: the worker's graceful shutdown is wired
to SIGTERM/SIGINT, and the stop signal a Windows container gets never reaches that handler. Only
Ctrl+C (`CTRL_C_EVENT`) triggers a drain on Windows today.

For production we recommend Linux containers (`deployment-docker`), and making jobs safe to repeat
in the meantime (`troubleshooting-duplicates`). Closing as a duplicate of #16. Please add a
reaction there.

title: 3.0 preview: override retries per Flow step
body:
Still playing with Flows on the 3.0 preview. A step takes its retry policy from its job, which
is a problem when the same job is used in two flows with different needs. `send_welcome` should
retry 5 times in the onboarding flow, but in our re-engagement flow it's best-effort and
shouldn't retry at all.

Proposal:

```python
Flow("reengage", steps=[
    step(pick_segment),
    step(send_welcome, after="pick_segment", retries=0),
])
```

and the same for `timeout`.
author: zeta-runner

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Good call, we'd been going back and forth on this. Since a step is "a job in a particular place in
a graph", step-level overrides for `retries` and `timeout` make sense. Everything else (queue,
backoff) still comes from the job.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
On `main` now: `step(fn, after=..., name=..., timeout=..., retries=...)`. It'll be documented in
`flows-steps-and-state` and `flows-error-handling` for 3.0.0. Closing.

title: Docs: say clearly that Redis Cluster isn't supported
body:
Follow-up to #21. We lost most of a day before learning that Redis Cluster (sharded mode) isn't
supported, and the only place that says so is a comment on that issue. Please add it to the Redis
broker page, and ideally to the FAQ, so people find it before they provision a cluster.
author: sundial-ops

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Thanks, done. `broker-redis` now has a "Redis Cluster" note saying sharded mode isn't supported,
and why (atomic multi-key operations), and `faq` links to it. Closing.

title: Invoices emailed twice from a long batch job
body:
Our `send_invoice_batch` job renders and emails ~200 invoices per run. This morning several
customers got the same invoice twice. Full log excerpt below:

```text
2025-11-17T04:00:02Z INFO  orbit.worker  w-1 started job=01JA9V3M7Q send_invoice_batch attempt=1
2025-11-17T04:05:03Z INFO  orbit.worker  w-3 started job=01JA9V3M7Q send_invoice_batch attempt=1
2025-11-17T04:06:40Z INFO  billing.mailer sent invoice INV-20931 to jordan.blake@example.com (+1-555-0178), 77 Fictional Blvd, Springfield
2025-11-17T04:07:12Z WARN  orbit.worker  w-1 [ORB-1101] LeaseExpired job=01JA9V3M7Q queue=billing lease=300s
2025-11-17T04:09:55Z INFO  billing.mailer sent invoice INV-20931 to jordan.blake@example.com (+1-555-0178), 77 Fictional Blvd, Springfield
2025-11-17T04:09:55Z DEBUG billing.payments using key sk-test-FAKE-9c1e77b20a for charge lookup
```

PDF rendering uses a native library. Redis broker, `ORBIT_LEASE` not set. Is the Redis broker
handing out the same job twice?
author: basalt-bee

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
First: your log contains a customer's email, phone number and address, plus an API key. Please
edit them out and rotate the key. Issue history is public. See `security`.

This is the lease expiry case from #4. While the native PDF library holds the GIL, the worker
can't send heartbeats, the 300 s default lease runs out, and a second worker gets the job. The
first worker logs ORB-1101 when it tries to acknowledge.

What we'd do:

- **Split the batch:** one job per invoice. Each job is short, so a redelivery repeats one
  invoice at most, and the job can check "already sent?" for that invoice before emailing.
- Raise `ORBIT_LEASE` above the longest stretch a single render can block (see
  `environment-variables-2x`).
- Use the mail provider's idempotency token if it has one.

`troubleshooting-duplicates` has the full checklist. Closing as a duplicate of #4.

comments.author: basalt-bee
comments.body: Rotated the key and redacted the post. Splitting into per-invoice jobs now, thanks.

title: Upgrading 2.8.0 to 2.9.0 with jobs still in the queue?
body:
2.9.0 just came out. We have a steady stream of jobs and can't drain the queues. Is a rolling
upgrade from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0 safe with 2.8.0 producers and workers still running for a while? Any
config changes needed?
author: driftwood-api

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Yes, a rolling upgrade within 2.x is fine: 2.9.0 workers process jobs written by 2.8.0 producers,
and no config changes are required. Things you'll notice:

- **Deprecation warnings** at startup for `orbit.ini` settings whose name or meaning changes in
  3.0. They're informational; nothing changes behaviour on 2.9.
- **Python 3.12** is now supported.
- Several fixes from this tracker (the `--concurrency` precedence bug in #1, Postgres reconnects
  in #47, masked broker passwords in #38).

2.9.0 is the **last 2.x release**, with security fixes until end of life on 2026-12-31. Getting
to 2.9.0 is also the first step of the 3.x upgrade: 3.x workers read jobs written by 2.9.0
producers. See `changelog` and `migrating-2-to-3`.

comments.author: driftwood-api
comments.body: Rolled out this morning without a hitch. Thanks!

title: 2.9.0 dashboard: /workers returns 500 during rolling upgrade
body:
We upgraded the dashboard to 2.9.0 first and are rolling the workers over the next two days. The
Workers page now fails:

```text
2025-11-21T10:02:13Z ERROR orbit.dashboard GET /workers 500: KeyError: 'python_version'
  File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/dashboard/views/workers.py", line 61, in workers
    "python": rec["python_version"],
```

The other pages work. I assume 2.9 workers write a field that 2.8 workers don't?
author: granite-pixel

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Exactly right: 2.9.0 workers record their Python version, and the Workers view assumes every
record has it. The page recovers as soon as the last 2.8.0 worker is gone (worker records expire
shortly after a worker stops heartbeating).

Since 2.9.0 is the last 2.x release and only gets security fixes from here, we won't ship a 2.x
patch for this. The 3.x dashboard handles missing fields. Workaround: upgrade workers before the
dashboard, or live without the Workers page during the rollout.

comments.author: granite-pixel
comments.body: Rollout finished and the page is back. Fine by us.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Thanks for confirming. Closing (won't fix on 2.x).

title: 2.9 broke everything??
body: upgraded to 2.9 and now logs are full of warnings. is it broken???
author: aster-yak

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Can you paste a few of the warning lines? Jobs still running, or are they failing too?

comments.author: aster-yak
comments.body:
jobs are running fine. it's lines like this, one per worker start:

```text
2025-11-24T09:00:01Z WARN  orbit.config  orbit.ini [orbit] lease: deprecated, becomes [worker] lease_seconds in 3.0 (see migrating-2-to-3)
2025-11-24T09:00:01Z WARN  orbit.config  orbit.ini [orbit] concurrency: deprecated, becomes [worker] concurrency in 3.0 (see migrating-2-to-3)
```

Nothing is broken. 2.9.0 added these deprecation warnings on purpose, for `orbit.ini` settings

title: SQS on EKS: ORB-1002 ExpiredTokenException after about an hour
body:
Workers on EKS use IAM roles for service accounts (web identity credentials). Everything works
for roughly an hour after a pod starts, then every SQS call fails until the pod is restarted:

```text
2025-11-26T10:58:41Z INFO  orbit.worker  orbit 2.9.0 worker w-eks-4 starting
2025-11-26T10:58:42Z INFO  orbit.broker  connected sqs://us-east-1/orbit-prod
2025-11-26T11:58:44Z ERROR orbit.broker.sqs [ORB-1002] BrokerAuthError: ExpiredTokenException: The security token included in the request is expired
2025-11-26T11:58:46Z ERROR orbit.broker.sqs [ORB-1002] BrokerAuthError: ExpiredTokenException: The security token included in the request is expired
```

Other services in the same cluster using the AWS SDK with the same mechanism refresh credentials
fine. It looks like the worker resolves credentials once at startup and never again.
author: rust-meadow

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Your diagnosis is right. The 2.x SQS broker resolves credentials once when it creates its client
and copies them out, so it loses the SDK's automatic refresh. With instance profiles the window is
long enough that few people notice. With web identity credentials it's about an hour.

This is fixed on `main` for 3.0, where the broker keeps the SDK's refreshable credentials. 2.9.0
is the last 2.x release and only gets security fixes, so there won't be a 2.x patch. Workarounds:

- restart workers before the credentials expire (for example a scheduled rollout restart), or
- use the node's instance profile for the worker pods instead of web identity credentials.

`broker-sqs` covers the credential chain.

comments.author: rust-meadow
comments.body: We'll do a 45-minute rollout restart until 3.0. Thanks for the clear answer.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Fixed in 3.0.0. Closing.

title: Retry only on specific exceptions
body:
Some failures are worth retrying (timeouts, 503s), others never will succeed (validation errors,
a 404 for a deleted record). Today every exception is retried until the policy runs out, so a
bad record burns all its attempts with backoff before landing in the DLQ an hour later.

Proposal:

```python
@app.job(retries=5, backoff="exponential", retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError))
def sync_record(record_id: str): ...
```

Anything not in `retry_on` would go to the DLQ immediately.
author: fjord-cache

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
This comes up a lot, and we agree with the idea. The open questions are naming
(`retry_on` vs. a `no_retry` list) and how it interacts with lease redeliveries, which aren't
exceptions at all. We'll pick it up after 3.0, so keeping it open.

Pattern for today: catch the errors you know are permanent inside the job, record them somewhere
you can see (a table, a log line, an alert), and return normally. The job then succeeds and
isn't retried. Only let retryable exceptions escape. See `retries-and-backoff`.

comments.author: pebble-queue
comments.body: +1, we have exactly the same wrapper in three services.

title: Docker docs: add a healthcheck example using `orbit doctor`
body:
The installation page mentions that `orbit doctor` exits non-zero when a check fails and can be
used as a readiness check, but the Docker deployment page has no healthcheck. A copy-pasteable
Compose example would help, including sensible intervals (I assume we shouldn't hit the broker
every second).
author: velvet-ion

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Good idea. `deployment-docker` now has:

```yaml
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "orbit", "doctor"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
```

with a note that each run opens a broker connection, so intervals under ~15 s aren't
recommended on large fleets. Closing.

title: CLI: respect NO_COLOR / don't print ANSI codes when not a TTY
body:
In CI logs, `orbit doctor` output is full of escape sequences:

```text
orbit 2.9.0 (python 3.12.11)
broker_url   redis://redis:6379/0   (env ORBIT_BROKER_URL)
^[[32m[ok]^[[0m broker reachable
```

Most CLIs check `isatty()` and the `NO_COLOR` environment variable. Could Orbit do the same?
author: ember-ci

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Agreed. The 3.x CLI on `main` already disables colour when stdout isn't a TTY and respects
`NO_COLOR`. Since 2.9.0 only gets security fixes now, we won't change 2.x. Workaround in CI:

```bash
orbit doctor | sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g'
```

`cli-reference` will list `NO_COLOR` for 3.x.

comments.author: ember-ci

title: 3.0 preview: flow run stays `running` forever after its run record is evicted
body:
On the 3.0 preview, my local Redis runs with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` (left over from using
it as a cache). During a load test some flow runs never finish:

```text
$ orbit flows status 01JBQ7H3SZ
run 01JBQ7H3SZ (onboarding)  state=running  started 2025-12-05T09:12:04Z
  create_account   succeeded
  send_welcome     pending
  assign_plan      pending
```

title: ORB-2001 for identical arguments when dict keys are in a different order
body:
Two services enqueue the same subscription sync with the same idempotency key. The arguments are
equal, but the second enqueue is rejected:

```python
# service A
sync_subscription.enqueue(sub_id="sub_8812", plan={"tier": "pro", "seats": 5})
# service B, a few seconds later
sync_subscription.enqueue(sub_id="sub_8812", plan={"seats": 5, "tier": "pro"})
```

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/billing/sync.py", line 92, in on_plan_changed
    sync_subscription.enqueue(sub_id=sub.id, plan=plan)
  File "/srv/billing/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/job.py", line 162, in enqueue
    self._check_idempotency(key, payload)
orbit.errors.IdempotencyConflict: [ORB-2001] idempotency key 'sub_8812' for sync_subscription already used with different arguments
```

The only difference is the key order in `plan`. We expected the second enqueue to be silently
deduplicated.
author: quartz-moth

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Confirmed. 2.x compares the serialized arguments byte for byte, and dict key order survives JSON
serialization, so equal dicts in a different order look different. They should be compared in a
canonical form (sorted keys).

It's fixed on `main` for 3.0. 2.9.0 only gets security fixes, so there won't be a 2.x patch.
Workaround: normalise dicts before enqueueing, recursively if they're nested:

```python
def canonical(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: canonical(obj[k]) for k in sorted(obj)}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [canonical(v) for v in obj]
    return obj

sync_subscription.enqueue(sub_id=sub.id, plan=canonical(plan))
```

See `idempotency`.

comments.author: quartz-moth
comments.body: The helper works for us. Thanks.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Fixed in 3.0.0. Closing.

title: Can I cancel a delayed job before a worker picks it up?
body:
We enqueue report exports with a `delay` so users can change their mind for a few minutes:

```python
handle = export_account.enqueue(account_id="acc_3381", delay="5m")
# store handle.id on the export row
```

If the user hits "cancel" in our UI before the delay is up, how do I tell Orbit to drop the job? I looked through the job handle and the CLI and couldn't find anything.

Right now we set a `cancelled` flag in our own DB and check it at the top of the job. That works, but every cancelled export still costs a worker slot and shows up as "succeeded" in our metrics. Is there a better way?

Running 2.9.0 with the Redis broker.
author: cobalt-wren

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
There's no cancel API in 2.x, and nothing in the 3.0 line that's about to ship either. The flag-in-your-DB approach is what we recommend today: check it when the job starts (and between chunks of work for long jobs) and return early. `api-reference-job` lists everything a handle can do.

A cancel API is tracked as a feature request in #34, so please add your use case there. Cancelling a *queued* job is cheap on Redis and Postgres but awkward on SQS, where you can't delete a message you haven't received yet. Any API would need to behave the same on all three brokers, so it would likely be "mark as cancelled, skip on delivery" under the hood.

Closing as answered.

comments.body: Same use case for scheduled reminder emails, added a +1 on #34. Even a skip-on-delivery implementation would be fine for us as long as the job ends up in a distinct "cancelled" state instead of "succeeded".

title: rediss:// broker URL fails with ORB-1001 CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED against private CA
body:
Our Redis is behind TLS with a certificate issued by an internal CA. `redis-cli --tls --cacert`
works from the same container, and so does a plain `redis.Redis.from_url(...)` in a Python shell.
Orbit workers never connect.

Environment:

- orbit 2.9.0, Python 3.10.13, Debian bookworm image
- `ORBIT_BROKER_URL=rediss://orbit-worker@redis.internal.example.com:6380/0`
- `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/internal/ca-bundle.pem` (this is what makes the plain redis-py client work)

Worker log:

```text
2026-01-05T14:21:07Z INFO  orbit.worker  orbit 2.9.0 worker w-a1c9 starting
2026-01-05T14:21:07Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 1 connecting to redis.internal.example.com:6380. [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate (_ssl.c:1006) (attempt 1)
2026-01-05T14:21:09Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 1 connecting to redis.internal.example.com:6380. [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate (_ssl.c:1006) (attempt 2)
2026-01-05T14:21:13Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 1 connecting to redis.internal.example.com:6380. [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate (_ssl.c:1006) (attempt 3)
```

`orbit doctor` reports the same error. Looks like Orbit builds its own SSL context and ignores
`SSL_CERT_FILE`?
author: harbor-node

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Yes, that's what's happening. The 2.9 Redis broker creates the connection pool with an explicit
SSL context and doesn't fall back to `SSL_CERT_FILE`. The URL is passed through to redis-py,
though, so you can point it at the CA bundle with the redis-py query parameter:

```text
ORBIT_BROKER_URL=rediss://orbit-worker@redis.internal.example.com:6380/0?ssl_ca_certs=/etc/ssl/internal/ca-bundle.pem
```

Please don't use `ssl_cert_reqs=none` as a workaround, which turns off verification entirely.
`troubleshooting-broker` covers the other common ORB-1001 causes. I'll add the TLS case there.

comments.author: harbor-node
comments.body: `ssl_ca_certs` in the URL works, workers are connected. Thanks! Fine to close from my side.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Closing with the workaround. 2.9.0 is the last 2.x release, so the env var fallback won't be
backported. The 3.x broker uses the default SSL context unless you configure otherwise.

title: Does the order of --queues give the first queue precedence?
body:
We run one worker pool for everything:

```bash
orbit worker --queues high,default,bulk --concurrency 12
```

I assumed listing `high` first means the worker drains `high` before touching `default` and
`bulk`. But during a big `bulk` backfill yesterday our `high` jobs (password reset emails) waited
several minutes. Is the order supposed to matter? If not, what's the recommended way to make sure
`high` is always served first?

orbit 2.9.0, Redis broker.
author: maple-queue

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
The order doesn't matter. A worker polls its queues round-robin with equal weight, so
`--queues high,default,bulk` and `--queues bulk,default,high` behave the same. That's deliberate:
strict ordering lets one busy queue starve the others completely.

What you saw is one third of every free slot going to `bulk`, and each slot being held for as long
as a backfill job runs. Two fixes, which you can combine:

- Give `high` dedicated capacity: one small pool with `--queues high` only, and the shared pool
  with `--queues high,default,bulk` that can help out when idle.
- Keep backfills from hogging slots: shorter jobs, or a separate pool for `bulk`.

`concepts-queues-priorities` explains queues vs. per-job `priority`. `scaling-workers` has a
worked example of the two-pool setup.

comments.author: maple-queue
comments.body:
Makes sense, thanks. We split out a 4-slot `high`-only pool and the reset emails are back to
sub-second. Closing.

title: ORB-1201 error message includes full argument values, so customer PII ends up in our logs
body:
When an enqueue fails JSON serialization, the exception message contains the **entire** argument
dict, not just the offending field. That message then goes to our log aggregator and to Sentry.
We found customer contact details in Sentry this morning because of it.

Repro (a `datetime` slipped into the payload):

```python
send_receipt.enqueue(order_id=order.id, customer=customer_payload)
```

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/shop/app/orders/views.py", line 88, in checkout
    send_receipt.enqueue(order_id=order.id, customer=customer_payload)
  File "/srv/shop/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/orbit/job.py", line 214, in enqueue
    payload = self._serialize(args, kwargs)
  File "/srv/shop/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/orbit/job.py", line 301, in _serialize
    raise SerializationError(msg)
orbit.errors.SerializationError: ORB-1201 SerializationError: arguments for job 'send_receipt' are not JSON-serializable: {'order_id': 'A-2291', 'customer': {'name': 'Jane Roe', 'email': 'jane.roe@example.com', 'phone': '555-0142', 'address': '1428 Elm Street, Apt 3, Springfield', 'created': datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 13, 17, 2, 41)}}
```

(The values above are from our staging seed data, but production looks exactly the same.)

**Expected:** the message names the argument and the type that failed, e.g.
`argument 'customer.created' is not JSON-serializable (datetime)`, and doesn't echo values.

We know we shouldn't be passing the whole customer record and are fixing that on our side, but a
library error message shouldn't dump arbitrary payloads.
author: saffron-ops

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Agreed, this is a bug. An error message shouldn't be a data exfiltration path. Thanks for
flagging that the values are seed data. Anyone else posting tracebacks here, please scrub real
customer data first.

Plan: the message will name the path of the first offending value and its type, and never include
values. That change goes into 3.0.0. For 2.9.0 (the last 2.x release) the workaround is to catch
`SerializationError` around `enqueue()` and log `type(exc).__name__` only.

Also +1 to the change you're making on your side. `security` has a section on keeping PII and
secrets out of job arguments, since they also sit in the broker, the DLQ and the dashboard.

comments.author: saffron-ops
comments.body: Thanks. We've added the wrapper and moved to passing `customer_id` only.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Shipped in 3.0.0. The message is now `argument 'customer.created' is not JSON-serializable
(datetime)`. Closing.

title: Support Redis Cluster (CROSSSLOT errors on managed Redis in cluster mode)
body:
Our platform team is moving all Redis to a managed offering that only runs in cluster mode.
Pointing Orbit at the cluster endpoint fails as soon as a worker starts:

```text
redis.exceptions.ResponseError: CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot
```

I assume the broker uses multi-key commands / Lua scripts across a queue's keys. Would you
consider supporting Redis Cluster, e.g. by putting all keys of a queue under one hash tag like
`{orbit:default}`? That would keep each queue on a single slot and still spread different
queues across shards.

We'd be willing to help test, and possibly contribute if there's a design you'd accept.
author: marble-fern

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Correct, the Redis broker relies on multi-key operations within a queue, and Redis Cluster isn't
supported in 2.x or in the upcoming 3.0. `broker-redis` lists standalone and Sentinel as the
supported topologies.

Hash-tagging per queue is the approach we'd take too. The catch is result keys and flow run
records, which are not per-queue. A design would need to cover those. If you want to write up a
short proposal, `contributing` describes the RFC process. Marking as a feature request.

comments.author: marble-fern
comments.body: Understood. I'll draft something covering queues, results and the DLQ and link it here.

title: Postgres broker: jobs wait up to 5 s before pickup under load while workers sit idle
body:
We use the Postgres broker (Postgres 15, workers connect directly with no pooler). At normal
traffic jobs start within ~100 ms. During our nightly import, when we enqueue ~400 jobs/s for about
ten minutes, a chunk of jobs sit in the queue for several seconds even though workers are idle.

What I measured over one import (time from enqueue to start):

| Percentile | Quiet hours | During import |
|---|---|---|
| p50 | 60 ms | 90 ms |
| p95 | 140 ms | 4.1 s |
| p99 | 210 ms | 5.0 s |

No errors anywhere, nothing in the DLQ, and every job eventually runs. With debug logging the
worker looks like it isn't being woken up and only finds work on its periodic poll:

```text
2026-01-20T02:14:03Z DEBUG orbit.broker.postgres listening on channel orbit_jobs
2026-01-20T02:14:03Z DEBUG orbit.broker.postgres poll queue=default fetched=0
2026-01-20T02:14:08Z DEBUG orbit.broker.postgres poll queue=default fetched=10
2026-01-20T02:14:08Z DEBUG orbit.broker.postgres poll queue=default fetched=10
2026-01-20T02:14:09Z DEBUG orbit.broker.postgres poll queue=default fetched=7
```

Between 02:14:03 and 02:14:08 there were about two thousand inserts into the queue but no wake-ups. Is
LISTEN/NOTIFY supposed to keep up at this rate?

orbit 2.9.0, Python 3.11.7, 6 workers × concurrency 8.
author: pg-wrangler

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Thanks for the numbers. This is very helpful. I can reproduce something similar with a synthetic
burst of inserts. Jobs are delayed, not lost: the poll always picks them up, which matches what
you see.

Working theory: while the listener connection is busy (or when a lot of notifications arrive at
once), wake-ups get missed and the worker falls back to its poll interval. We don't have a fix yet.
For now:

- Make sure nothing sits between workers and Postgres in transaction pooling mode. `LISTEN` is
  session-scoped. You said you connect directly, so that's not it in your case.
- Avoid very long transactions on the jobs table during the import.

`broker-postgres` describes how the broker combines polling with LISTEN/NOTIFY. Keeping this open
while we investigate.

comments.author: pg-wrangler
comments.body:
Confirmed nothing in between, and the import commits in batches of 500. Happy to run a debug build
if that helps.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Added a section on this to `troubleshooting-broker` so people searching for "Postgres jobs delayed"
land here. Still under investigation.

title: DeprecationWarning: datetime.utcnow() floods test output on Python 3.12
body:
On Python 3.12 every enqueue and every worker heartbeat emits:

```text
/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/broker/base.py:57: DeprecationWarning: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and scheduled for removal in a future version. Use timezone-aware objects to represent datetimes in UTC: datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC).
  now = datetime.utcnow()
```

Our CI runs pytest with `-W error::DeprecationWarning`, so every test that enqueues a job fails.
Not a functional problem, just noise (and a CI blocker for us). orbit 2.9.0.
author: dune-sprocket

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Thanks. The 3.0 line already uses timezone-aware datetimes throughout, so this goes away when you
upgrade. 2.9.0 is the last 2.x release and only gets security fixes (see the supported versions
table in `security`), so we won't patch this on 2.x.

To keep `-W error` for your own code, filter just this warning from Orbit's modules in your pytest

```ini

    error::DeprecationWarning
    ignore:datetime.datetime.utcnow:DeprecationWarning:orbit
```

comments.author: dune-sprocket
comments.body: The filter does the job, thanks. Closing.

title: Retry only on specific exception types
body:
Today a job decorated with `retries=5` retries on *any* exception. For our payment jobs that's
wrong in both directions:

- `ValueError` / validation errors will fail the same way five times, so retrying them only delays
  the DLQ entry by several minutes of exponential backoff.
- Network timeouts are exactly what we want to retry.

**Proposal:** an allow-list (and maybe a deny-list) on the decorator, something like:

```python
@app.job(retries=5, backoff="exponential", retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError))
def capture_payment(payment_id: str): ...
```

Anything not listed would go straight to the DLQ with `RetryExhausted` after the first attempt.

Current workaround: we catch the non-retryable errors, log them and `return` so the job is marked
as succeeded, which hides real failures from the dashboard.
author: copper-kite

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Reasonable request, and it's the same one as #72 (`retry_on`), which is still open. I'm closing this as a duplicate so the design discussion stays in one place, and I've copied two notes from your write-up there:

- Sending a non-retryable failure straight to the DLQ (instead of returning) is better than the current workaround, because the failure stays visible and replayable with `orbit dlq replay`.
- In 3.x it has to compose with the global `[retries]` policy, so a per-job list would override it, not merge with it.

`retries-and-backoff` documents the current behaviour.

comments.author: velvet-ion
comments.body: Added a +1 on #72. We'd use the deny-list form more than the allow-list form.

title: Postgres broker: allow Orbit's tables to live in a dedicated schema
body:
Our DBAs require every application component to keep its tables in its own schema, not in
`public`. As far as I can tell the Postgres broker always creates and queries its tables in
whatever the connection's default schema is.

Could the broker accept a schema name, so that `orbit` tables can sit next to the app's tables in
the same database but in a separate namespace? We'd also like to grant the worker role access to
that schema only.
author: quillfeather

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
The broker uses unqualified table names, so it follows the connection's `search_path`. You can
set that per connection with the standard libpq `options` parameter in the URL. URL-encoded, it
looks like this:

```text
ORBIT_BROKER_URL=postgresql://orbit_worker@pg.internal.example.com:5432/app?options=-csearch_path%3Dorbit
```

Create the `orbit` schema first and grant the worker role `USAGE`/`CREATE` on it. That covers the
isolation part today. A first-class setting would still be nicer, especially for docs and
`orbit doctor` output, so I'm keeping this open as a feature request for 3.x. See `broker-postgres`
for the current connection options.

comments.author: quillfeather
comments.body: The `search_path` option works for us in staging. +1 for a proper setting later.

title: How should I pass a date to a job? Getting ORB-1201 SerializationError
body:
I'm new to Orbit. I have a monthly invoice job that takes the end of the billing period:

```python
@app.job(retries=3)
def generate_invoice(invoice_id: str, period_end: date): ...

generate_invoice.enqueue(invoice_id="INV-3307", period_end=date(2026, 1, 31))
```

The enqueue call raises:

```text
orbit.errors.SerializationError: ORB-1201 SerializationError: arguments for job 'generate_invoice' are not JSON-serializable: {'invoice_id': 'INV-3307', 'period_end': datetime.date(2026, 1, 31)}
```

Is there a way to register a custom encoder for dates, or am I supposed to convert everything
myself? (orbit 2.9.0)
author: juniper-io

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Convert it yourself. Job arguments are stored in the broker as plain JSON, and Orbit deliberately
checks this at enqueue time so the failure shows up in the caller rather than on a worker later.
There's no custom-encoder hook.

The usual pattern is ISO-8601 strings in, parse at the top of the job:

```python
@app.job(retries=3)
def generate_invoice(invoice_id: str, period_end: str):
    period_end = date.fromisoformat(period_end)
    ...

generate_invoice.enqueue(invoice_id="INV-3307", period_end="2026-01-31")
```

Same for `set` (use a list), `Decimal` (use a string) and ORM objects (pass the primary key).
See the "Arguments must be JSON" section of `concepts-jobs`.

comments.author: juniper-io
comments.body: Got it, ISO strings it is. Thanks!

title: `orbit dlq list` should support machine-readable (JSON) output

**Request:** a JSON (or JSON Lines) output mode for `orbit dlq list`, one object per entry with at

pipe it straight into `jq`.

Bonus: the same output mode for `orbit flows status` once 3.0 is out.

match what the dashboard API already has. `cli-reference` will document it once it exists.

comments.body:
Sorry about that paragraph. It was pasted in from a "test your triage bot" template one of our
interns was playing with, and I didn't notice. The feature request is real though.

title: orbit slow?
body: our jobs are really slow with orbit. is there a setting to make it faster?
author: zeta-runner

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Happy to help, but "slow" could mean a few different things. Could you tell us:

- Orbit version and broker
- How many workers you run and with what `--concurrency` (or `ORBIT_CONCURRENCY` on 2.x)
- Is the time spent *waiting in the queue* or *running the job*? The dashboard shows both.
- Roughly how many jobs per second you enqueue and what a typical job does

comments.author: zeta-runner
comments.body:
2.9.0 with redis. 4 worker containers with ORBIT_CONCURRENCY=2. we enqueue maybe 50 jobs/sec at
peak. each job calls a partner API, takes about 1s. jobs wait in the queue for minutes at peak.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
That explains it. 4 workers × 2 slots = 8 jobs running at once. At ~1 s per job that's about
8 jobs/s of capacity against 50 jobs/s of arrivals, so the queue can only grow during peaks.

Your jobs are I/O-bound (waiting on an HTTP call), so you can raise concurrency a lot further than
your CPU count. Something like `ORBIT_CONCURRENCY=16` on the same 4 containers gives you 64 slots.
Watch the partner API's rate limits, and check memory per worker as you go.

`scaling-workers` has the capacity arithmetic and `performance-tuning` covers the other knobs.
Closing as answered, but feel free to follow up here.

title: Docs: explain how idempotency_key works with SQS (and FIFO deduplication)
body:
The `idempotency` page explains keys with Redis examples only, and the `broker-sqs` page doesn't
mention idempotency at all. We're moving from Redis to SQS and I can't work out from the docs:

1. Is `idempotency_key` enforced at all on the SQS broker, and if so where is the key stored?
2. SQS FIFO queues have their own `MessageDeduplicationId`. Does Orbit set it from the idempotency
   key? Do I need both?
3. FIFO deduplication only lasts five minutes. What happens to a duplicate enqueue that arrives
   after that?
4. On a standard (non-FIFO) queue, what's the recommended pattern?

A short section on each broker page, or an SQS-specific part of `idempotency`, would really help.
author: tidepool-io

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Fair point, this is a gap. The short answer to (3) is the important one: SQS's FIFO deduplication
window is five minutes, so it is **not** a substitute for Orbit's idempotency keys. Don't rely on
it for anything that can be retried or re-sent later.

We'll write up the rest properly (where the key lives with SQS, FIFO vs. standard, and how it
interacts with redeliveries) in `idempotency` and link to it from `broker-sqs`. Keeping this open
until that's done.

comments.author: tidepool-io
comments.body: Thanks, that already helps. Subscribing.

title: ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError when the Redis password contains @ or #
body:
After our Redis password was rotated, workers can't authenticate. The new password contains `@`
and `#`. The env var looks like this (password replaced with a fake one with the same characters):

```text
ORBIT_BROKER_URL=redis://orbit:p@ss#w0rd-FAKE@redis.internal.example.com:6379/0
```

```text
2026-02-13T08:41:57Z INFO  orbit.worker  orbit 2.9.0 worker w-02bd starting
2026-02-13T08:41:57Z ERROR orbit.broker.redis ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError: WRONGPASS invalid username-password pair or user is disabled.
```

`redis-cli --user orbit --pass 'p@ss#w0rd-FAKE'` works fine. Is there a way to quote the password,
or do we need to ask for a new one without special characters?
author: ember-ci

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
The broker URL is parsed as a URL, so reserved characters in the password must be
percent-encoded: `@` → `%40`, `#` → `%23`. With your example:

```text
ORBIT_BROKER_URL=redis://orbit:p%40ss%23w0rd-FAKE@redis.internal.example.com:6379/0
```

Unencoded, the `#` starts a URL fragment, and everything after it gets dropped. `python -c "import
urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote('p@ss#w0rd-FAKE', safe=''))"` prints the encoded form.
`environment-variables-2x` documents `ORBIT_BROKER_URL`, and the auth section of
`troubleshooting-broker` covers other ORB-1002 causes.

comments.author: ember-ci
comments.body: Percent-encoding fixed it. Thanks for the quick answer!

title: 3.0.0: `orbit worker --concurrency 8` is ignored when orbit.toml sets [worker] concurrency
body:

sets a default for all worker pools:

```toml
[worker]

prefetch = 10
```

A few pools need more slots, so they start with an explicit flag:


The startup log shows the toml value instead of the flag:

```text
2026-03-03T08:52:10Z INFO  orbit.worker  orbit 3.0.0 worker w-4c1d starting
2026-03-03T08:52:10Z INFO  orbit.worker  queues=default,high concurrency=4 prefetch=10
2026-03-03T08:52:10Z INFO  orbit.worker  lease_seconds=300 heartbeat_seconds=30
2026-03-03T08:52:10Z INFO  orbit.broker  connected redis://redis.internal.example.com:6379/0
```

comments.author: sam-okafor

Confirmed, and you're right about the expected order: a flag on the command line beats

title: Como migrar variáveis ORBIT_* para orbit.toml? O migrate-config só lê orbit.ini
body:
Olá! Estamos migrando da 2.9 para a 3.0.0. No nosso cluster Kubernetes toda a configuração do
Orbit é feita por variáveis de ambiente no Deployment:

```yaml
env:
  - name: ORBIT_BROKER_URL
    value: redis://redis-filas.svc.example.com:6379/1
  - name: ORBIT_CONCURRENCY
    value: "12"
  - name: ORBIT_LEASE
    value: "900"
```

Não temos nenhum `orbit.ini`. Tentei rodar `orbit migrate-config orbit.ini` e, claro, deu "arquivo
não encontrado". Depois do upgrade, o worker ignora as variáveis e tenta conectar em localhost.

Qual é o caminho recomendado nesse caso? Preciso escrever o `orbit.toml` à mão? Existe uma tabela
de equivalência entre as variáveis e as chaves novas?

Versões: Orbit 3.0.0, Python 3.11.8.

Obrigado!
author: rafa-filas

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Olá! (Replying in English, I hope that's OK.)

Right, `orbit migrate-config` only converts an `orbit.ini` file. 3.x no longer reads the
`ORBIT_*` variables, which is why the worker falls back to the default broker on localhost. For an
env-only setup you write `orbit.toml` by hand. It's short:

| 2.x env var | `orbit.toml` |
|---|---|
| `ORBIT_BROKER_URL` | `[broker] url` |
| `ORBIT_CONCURRENCY` | `[worker] concurrency` |
| `ORBIT_LEASE` | `[worker] lease_seconds` (still seconds) |

```toml
[broker]
url = "redis://redis-filas.svc.example.com:6379/1"

[worker]
concurrency = 12
lease_seconds = 900
```

In Kubernetes the usual approach is to put this in a ConfigMap (or a Secret if the URL has a
password) mounted where the worker starts, then check it with `orbit doctor`. If you'd rather keep
the URL in an env var, read it yourself and pass `Orbit(broker=os.environ[...])`. An explicit
`broker=` argument takes precedence over the file.

See `migrating-2-to-3`, `environment-variables-2x` and `configuration-reference`.

comments.author: rafa-filas
comments.body:
Perfeito, funcionou com o ConfigMap e o `orbit doctor` passou. Seria ótimo se o migrate-config
aceitasse as variáveis de ambiente também, mas por enquanto está resolvido. Obrigado!

title: migrate-config fails with ORB-1801 when orbit.ini contains a % (percent-encoded password)
body:
Our broker password contains an `@`, so per the docs the URL in `orbit.ini` is percent-encoded:

```ini
[orbit]
broker_url = redis://orbit:hunter%40FAKE@redis.internal.example.com:6379/0
```

2.9.0 reads this file fine. `orbit migrate-config` on 3.0.0 refuses it:

```text
$ orbit migrate-config orbit.ini
error: [ORB-1801] ConfigMigrationError: could not convert orbit.ini: '%' must be followed by '%' or '(', found: '%40FAKE@redis.internal.example.com:6379/0'
```

That message looks like Python's `configparser` interpolation. Doubling it to `%%40` makes
`migrate-config` happy, but then the generated `orbit.toml` contains `%40` (correct). I just don't
want to edit the 2.x file that's still used by the old deployment.
author: cobalt-wren

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Thanks, good catch. `migrate-config` reads the ini with interpolation turned on, while the 2.x
runtime reads it without. They should agree, so this is a bug in the converter.

Workaround: copy the file, double the `%` in the copy only, and run `orbit migrate-config` on the
copy. The output is correct, as you saw. We'll switch the converter to raw reads. See
`migrating-2-to-3` for the rest of the conversion steps.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Fixed in 3.0.3: `migrate-config` now reads `orbit.ini` without interpolation. Closing.

title: How do I send traces to an OpenTelemetry collector in 3.0?
body:
We run an OpenTelemetry collector as a sidecar on every worker pod (`otel-collector:4317`). What's
the minimum config to get Orbit 3.0 to export job spans to it? I see a `[telemetry]` section in
the configuration reference but no complete example. Do I need an extra package?
author: lumen-dev

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Two things:

1. Install the extra: `pip install "orbit[redis,otel]"` (keep whichever broker extra you already
   use).
2. Add a `[telemetry]` section:

```toml
[telemetry]
otlp_endpoint = "http://otel-collector:4317"
service_name = "billing-workers"
```

That's all. Workers then export spans for the jobs they run, with the job and queue names as
attributes. `observability-tracing` shows what the spans contain. `configuration-reference` lists the two keys.

comments.author: lumen-dev
comments.body: Works, spans are showing up. Thanks!

title: [telemetry] service_name is ignored for traces: spans show unknown_service:python
body:
With this config on 3.0.0:

```toml
[telemetry]
otlp_endpoint = "http://otel-collector.observability.svc:4317"
service_name = "orders-workers"
```

metrics arrive in our backend with `service.name = orders-workers`, but every **trace** span has
`service.name = unknown_service:python`. All Orbit services end up merged under one name in the
tracing UI.

Setting `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=orders-workers` in the environment fixes traces, so it looks like
`service_name` is only applied to the meter provider and not to the tracer provider.
author: maple-queue

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Reproduced. The resource built from `service_name` is passed to the meter provider and not to the
tracer provider. `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` is the right workaround until the fix ships, since the
OpenTelemetry SDK picks it up by default. `observability-tracing` will get a note.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Fixed in 3.0.3. Traces and metrics now share the same resource. Closing.

title: upgraded to 3.0 and now nothing works
body: pip upgraded orbit over the weekend and now nothing runs. rolled back to the old image for now.
author: byte-heron

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Sorry about the surprise. 3.0 is a major release with breaking changes, and it's worth pinning
your Orbit version so a rebuild can't jump a major version (`installation` shows how).

To figure out what broke, could you share the worker log from the 3.0 image, especially anything
with an `ORB-` code, and how you configure Orbit today (`orbit.ini`, environment variables,
both)? `migrating-2-to-3` lists everything that changed.

comments.author: byte-heron
comments.body:
we have an orbit.ini plus ORBIT_BROKER_URL set in the container. on 3.0 the worker says it's
connecting to localhost and just keeps retrying. no other errors.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
That's the cause. 3.x reads its settings from `orbit.toml` only. It ignores `orbit.ini` and the
`ORBIT_*` variables, so it falls back to the default broker on localhost. Steps:

```bash
orbit migrate-config orbit.ini      # writes orbit.toml next to it
orbit doctor                        # checks broker, config and versions
```

Double-check that the generated file has the broker URL you currently set in `ORBIT_BROKER_URL`.
The env var is not part of the conversion.

title: Flow step fails with ORB-1202 *after* it finished, and retries repeat the whole expensive step
body:
We moved our monthly statements job to a 3.0 Flow. The `render_statements` step renders HTML
for every account in a batch and returns it so the next step (`upload_statements`) can push it to
storage.

The step does all its work (about 3.5 minutes), and *then* fails because the return value is too
big. It's retried with backoff, renders everything again, fails again, and ends up in the DLQ
after ~11 minutes of wasted CPU:

```text
2026-03-12T09:31:07Z INFO  orbit.worker  job j_8e21c4 step=render_statements run=fr_01JR2M8K4T attempt=1/3 finished in 212.4s
2026-03-12T09:31:07Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1202 PayloadTooLarge: result of step 'render_statements' is 2,941 KB (max_payload_kb=512)
2026-03-12T09:31:08Z WARN  orbit.retries job j_8e21c4 attempt 1/3 failed, retrying in 12s
2026-03-12T09:34:52Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1202 PayloadTooLarge: result of step 'render_statements' is 2,941 KB (max_payload_kb=512)
2026-03-12T09:34:53Z WARN  orbit.retries job j_8e21c4 attempt 2/3 failed, retrying in 48s
2026-03-12T09:39:29Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1202 PayloadTooLarge: result of step 'render_statements' is 2,941 KB (max_payload_kb=512)
2026-03-12T09:39:29Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted: job j_8e21c4 moved to DLQ after 3 attempts
```

Two problems as I see it:

1. The size check happens after the work, so there's no early warning.
2. Retrying a result that is deterministically too large can never succeed.

orbit 3.0.0, Redis broker and Redis result backend.
author: ochre-moth

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed log. The limit itself is intended: step results go through the result
backend and are passed to later steps, so they're capped by `[limits] max_payload_kb` like any job
payload. The fix on your side is to write the HTML to storage inside `render_statements` and
return a reference (key + count). `flows-steps-and-state` has an example under "What a step may
return".

I agree that (2) is wasteful, though. Retrying `ORB-1202` on a step result is documented today
(`flows-error-handling` says it "rarely helps"), but sending it straight to the DLQ would be
better behaviour. Keeping this open to track that.

comments.author: ochre-moth
comments.body:
Returning a storage key works, and the flow is faster too since nothing big goes through Redis.
+1 on not retrying the size error.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Related: a cheap early check would be to log a warning when a step's result is over ~80% of
`max_payload_kb`, so people find out before they hit the limit. Adding that to the discussion.

title: How does a flow step get the return value of the step before it?
body:
Trying out Flows in 3.0.0 with the onboarding example:

```python
@app.job()
def create_account(user_id: str) -> dict:
    ...
    return {"account_id": "acc_9120"}

@app.job()
def send_welcome(user_id: str, account_id: str): ...

flow = Flow("onboarding", steps=[step(create_account), step(send_welcome, after="create_account")])
flow.run(user_id="u_42")
```

`send_welcome` fails on its first attempt with `TypeError: send_welcome() missing 1 required
positional argument: 'account_id'`. How am I supposed to get `account_id` from `create_account`
into `send_welcome`?
author: paper-crane-dev

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Orbit injects an upstream result into a parameter **named after the upstream step**, not after
the keys inside the result. So:

```python
@app.job()
def send_welcome(user_id: str, create_account: dict):
    account_id = create_account["account_id"]
    ...
```

`user_id` still comes from `flow.run(user_id=...)`. A parameter that matches neither a run input
nor an upstream step falls back to its default, and without a default you get exactly the
`TypeError` you saw. You can only inject results from steps in your own `after` chain, never from
a sibling. Details are in `flows-steps-and-state` under "Passing data between steps".

comments.author: paper-crane-dev
comments.body: That's the piece I missed. Works now, thank you.

title: ORB-1802 UnknownConfigKey for documented key [limits] max_payload_kb on 3.0.0
body:
We need slightly bigger payloads for one integration, so we added this to `orbit.toml`, copied
from the configuration reference:

```toml
[limits]
max_payload_kb = 1024
```

Workers now refuse to start:

```text
2026-03-16T07:55:02Z ERROR orbit.config ORB-1802 UnknownConfigKey: unknown key 'max_payload_kb' in section [limits] (orbit.toml:18)
```

`orbit doctor` agrees:

```text
✔ orbit 3.0.0, python 3.10.14
✘ config: ./orbit.toml (7 sections, 1 unknown keys)
    ORB-1802 UnknownConfigKey: [limits] max_payload_kb
✔ broker: redis://redis.internal.example.com:6379/0 reachable (redis 7.2.4, 1.1 ms)
1 check failed.
```

Removing the section makes it start again (with the default 512). Every other key we use is

author: saffron-ops

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Confirmed, sorry about that. The key validator in 3.0.0 is missing `[limits] max_payload_kb`,
even though the limit itself is enforced. That's why the default of 512 still applies when you
remove the section. Because unknown keys stop the worker from starting, I've marked this S2.

There's no workaround that lets you change the limit on 3.0.0. If you only need it for one
integration, consider passing a reference to the data instead of the data itself. It's usually
the better fix anyway (`performance-tuning`, "Keep payloads small").

comments.author: saffron-ops
comments.body: Fair. We'll stage the payload in object storage for now.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Fixed in 3.0.3: `max_payload_kb` is accepted again and `orbit doctor` reports it. Closing.

title: migrate-config: accept ORBIT_* environment variables as input
body:

`orbit migrate-config` only accepts an ini file, so for us it does nothing and we wrote

comments.author: rafa-filas

comments.body:

title: flow.run() raises ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable on the SQS broker
body:
Our jobs run on the SQS broker. I wanted to try Flows from 3.0, but starting a run fails
immediately:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/onboarding/start.py", line 14, in <module>
    run = onboarding.run(user_id="u_42")
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/orbit/flow.py", line 133, in run
    record = self._app.results.create_run(self, inputs)
orbit.errors.ResultBackendUnavailable: ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable: result backend 'redis' is not available: broker is 'sqs'
```

Our `orbit.toml` only has `[broker] url = "sqs://..."`. Do I need to configure something for
results? Can I point results at our existing Redis while keeping SQS as the broker?
author: harbor-pilot

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
The result backend uses the broker's connection, and the default is `backend = "redis"`, which
needs a Redis broker. That's the error you're seeing.

SQS has no matching result backend, and mixed setups (SQS broker + Redis results) aren't
supported. On SQS you should set:

```toml
[results]
backend = "none"
```

With `backend = "none"`, flows aren't available, since a flow run needs somewhere to keep its
state. So your options are:

- keep plain jobs on SQS and write any results you need to your own datastore, or
- run your flows on a separate Orbit app that uses a Redis or Postgres broker.

`results-backend` has an "SQS users" section that covers exactly this, and `broker-sqs` lists what
the SQS broker supports.

comments.author: harbor-pilot
comments.body: Clear, thanks. We'll run the onboarding flow on a small Redis-backed app.

title: cli-reference: states printed by `orbit flows status` aren't documented
body:
`cli-reference` lists `orbit flows status <run_id>` with a one-line description but doesn't say
what the output columns mean or which states a run and a step can be in. I saw `queued` and
`skipped` in our output and had to guess what they mean. A table of states (and maybe the exit
code when a run has failed) would help people writing scripts around it.
author: dev-ibis

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Good point. The states are described in `flows-overview` (`queued` = the step's job is on the
broker, `skipped` = an upstream step failed so this step will never run), but `cli-reference`
should be self-contained. I've added a states table and an annotated example of the output to the
`orbit flows status` entry. Closing.

title: `orbit flows status` shows step as running forever after ORB-1502 StepTimeout exhausts retries
body:
Our nightly CRM sync flow has a step with a 120s timeout. Last night it timed out on all three
attempts and went to the DLQ, which is fine, but the run never moved to a failed state:

```text
2026-03-21T02:14:09Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1502 StepTimeout: step 'sync_crm' exceeded timeout 120s (run fr_01JS0TZ5QW, attempt 3/3)
2026-03-21T02:14:09Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted: job j_51d9a0 moved to DLQ after 3 attempts
```

Five hours later:

```text
$ orbit flows status fr_01JS0TZ5QW
run fr_01JS0TZ5QW  flow=nightly-crm-sync  state=running  started=2026-03-21T02:00:00Z
  fetch_accounts   succeeded  attempts=1
  sync_crm         running    attempts=3
  notify_ops       pending    attempts=0
```

I expected `sync_crm failed`, `notify_ops skipped`, and the run `failed`. Our alerting checks for
failed runs, so this one was silent. When a step fails by *raising* instead of timing out, the
states are correct.

orbit 3.0.0, Python 3.12.2.
author: cron-jules

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Reproduced. When the last attempt ends with a timeout, the worker writes the DLQ entry but skips
the final state update on the run record. A raised exception goes through a different path,
which is why that case works. Marking S2 because it hides failures from monitoring.

The run isn't lost: fixing the cause and running `orbit dlq replay j_51d9a0` still resumes it, as
described in `flows-error-handling`. Until the fix ships, alert on `ORB-1301` for flow step jobs as
well as on failed runs.

comments.author: cron-jules
comments.body: Added an alert on ORB-1301 for now. Thanks for the quick look.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:

`skipped`. Closing.

title: Expose a Prometheus /metrics endpoint in addition to OTLP
body:
Most of our services are scraped by Prometheus directly. For Orbit we'd have to deploy an
OpenTelemetry collector just to translate OTLP metrics into something Prometheus can scrape.

Would you consider an optional built-in `/metrics` endpoint on the worker (queue depth, jobs
started/succeeded/failed, retry and DLQ counts, lease expiries)? Even a minimal version would let
smaller teams skip the collector.
author: maple-queue

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Today Orbit exports metrics over OTLP only (`[telemetry] otlp_endpoint`), and the recommended way
to get them into Prometheus is the collector's Prometheus exporter. `observability-metrics` has a
minimal collector config for that.

A built-in endpoint is a reasonable ask for small setups, but it means another HTTP listener in
every worker process, which some people won't want. Keeping this open as a feature request to
gauge interest. A +1 on the issue helps.

comments.author: copper-kite
comments.body: +1 from us. We run a dozen small deployments where a collector per environment is overkill.

title: Ship type hints for job .enqueue() (py.typed) so mypy can check job arguments
body:
With 3.0.1, `mypy --strict` treats everything imported from `orbit` as `Any`, because the package
doesn't ship a `py.typed` marker. The bigger win would be typing the decorator so that
`send_receipt.enqueue(order_id=123)` is flagged when `order_id: str`.

Rough idea:

- add `py.typed` and inline annotations for the public API (`Orbit`, `Flow`, `step`, job handles)
- make `@app.job` return a generic `Job[P, R]` whose `enqueue` takes `P.kwargs` plus the enqueue
  options (`priority`, `delay`, `queue`)

Even the first bullet alone would help a lot.
author: pg-wrangler

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
+1 on the first bullet; that's mostly mechanical, and we'd take a PR (`contributing` has the dev
setup). The second is harder: `enqueue` mixes the job's own kwargs with Orbit's options, so
`ParamSpec` alone can't express it cleanly when a job has a parameter called `delay` or
`priority`. We'd want a design note for that part. Leaving open.

title: `orbit migrate-config` silently drops the [retries] section (3.0.1)
body:
We're migrating our services one at a time. Services converted with 3.0.0 last week are fine. The
ones converted today with 3.0.1 have no `[retries]` section in the generated `orbit.toml`, and
there's no warning about it.

Input `orbit.ini`:

```ini
[orbit]
broker_url = redis://redis.internal.example.com:6379/2
concurrency = 16
lease = 900

[retries]
max_attempts = 8
backoff = exponential
max_delay_seconds = 1800
```

Output of `orbit migrate-config orbit.ini` on 3.0.1:

```toml
[broker]
url = "redis://redis.internal.example.com:6379/2"

[worker]
concurrency = 16
lease_seconds = 900
```

The command exits 0. Running the same file through 3.0.0 produces the `[retries]` section as
expected. Because nothing fails, the converted services quietly fall back to the default retry
policy, which is much less forgiving than ours.
author: tidepool-io

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Confirmed, and thank you for comparing against 3.0.0. That narrowed it down quickly. This is a
regression in 3.0.1: the section mapping in `migrate-config` was refactored and `[retries]` fell out
of the list of sections it copies. No error is raised because nothing is "wrong" with the input.

Impact: services converted with 3.0.1 use the defaults (`max_attempts = 3`,
`backoff = "exponential"`, `max_delay_seconds = 600`). Per-job `retries=` on the decorator still
applies. Jobs that exhaust the smaller budget end up in the DLQ earlier than you'd expect, with
`ORB-1301`.

Workaround: add the `[retries]` section to the generated file by hand, or convert with 3.0.0.
The fix is going into 3.0.3. `retries-and-backoff` lists the keys.

comments.author: tidepool-io
comments.body: Added it back by hand on the services we'd converted. We'll hold the rest until the fix is out.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
3.0.3 is out with the fix, and `migrate-config` now has a test that every 2.x section round-trips.
If you converted anything with 3.0.1, check it has a `[retries]` section (or just re-run the
conversion with 3.0.3). Noted in `changelog` and `migrating-2-to-3`. Closing.

title: orbit doctor fails: heartbeat_seconds (120) <= lease_seconds (300) / 3
body:
To cut down on broker traffic I raised the heartbeat interval. Now `orbit doctor` fails, and the
worker logs the same failed check at startup:

```text
$ orbit doctor
✔ orbit 3.0.1, python 3.11.8
✔ config: ./orbit.toml (6 sections, 0 unknown keys)
✔ broker: redis://redis.internal.example.com:6379/0 reachable (redis 7.2.4, 0.9 ms)
✔ results: redis backend reachable
✘ worker: heartbeat_seconds (120) <= lease_seconds (300) / 3
1 check failed.
```

What is this check protecting against? Is it safe to ignore if our jobs are short?
author: mossy-stack

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Don't ignore it. A worker's heartbeat is what renews the lease on the jobs it's running. With
`heartbeat_seconds = 120` and `lease_seconds = 300`, a running job gets at most two renewals per
lease window. If one heartbeat is late (GC pause, network blip, busy broker), the lease can lapse
and the job gets redelivered to another worker while the first one is still running it.

The check makes sure there are at least three heartbeats per lease, so that one or two missed
beats are survivable. Pick one:

- go back to `heartbeat_seconds = 30` (the default), or
- raise `lease_seconds` with it, e.g. `heartbeat_seconds = 120` with `lease_seconds = 600`. That
  means a crashed worker's jobs take longer to be picked up again.

Heartbeat traffic is usually tiny compared with job traffic. `performance-tuning` has numbers
under "Heartbeat cost" if you want to check before tuning it. The full explanation is in
`leases-and-heartbeats`.

comments.author: mossy-stack
comments.body:
Went back to 30s. The numbers in performance-tuning show it was never our bottleneck anyway.
Thanks.

title: Flows: dynamic fan-out (run a step once per item of an upstream result)
body:
Static fan-out with several steps sharing the same `after=` works nicely. What I can't express is
fan-out whose width is only known at runtime, e.g.:

1. `list_invoices` returns 0 to 2,000 invoice ids
2. `render_invoice` should run once **per id**, in parallel
3. `send_batch_summary` runs after all of them

Today I have `list_invoices` enqueue `render_invoice` jobs itself, but then the flow doesn't
know about them: no status in `orbit flows status`, no fan-in, and replaying from the DLQ doesn't
resume anything.

Something like `step(render_invoice, after="list_invoices", map_over="list_invoices")` would cover
it. Happy to discuss the API.
author: paper-crane-dev

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Agreed this is the most common thing people try after the basic examples. It's not supported in
3.0. The graph is fixed when the flow is defined, as `flows-steps-and-state` describes.

The hard parts are mostly about state: the run record would grow with every mapped item, which
runs into `max_payload_kb` and `ttl_days` limits, and replaying one failed item needs to resume
just that branch. If we do it, mapped results would likely be stored per item rather than in the
run record. Keeping open as a feature request. Use cases with typical fan-out widths are very
welcome here.

comments.author: ochre-moth
comments.body:
Our use case: 50-300 accounts per statement run. We'd only need the fan-in to see success/fail
counts, not the individual results.

body:

`orbit dashboard --port 7777` exits right away:

```text
2026-04-06T15:20:31Z INFO  orbit.dashboard starting on :7777 (auth=oidc)
2026-04-06T15:20:31Z ERROR orbit.dashboard ORB-1702 OIDCMisconfigured: could not fetch discovery document https://login.example.com/realms/ops/.well-known/openid-configuration (HTTP 404)
```

The client definitely exists. Here's what our IdP admin API returns for it:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-test-FAKE-9fQ2xL7mVb3Tq8Zr" \
  "https://login.example.com/auth/admin/realms/ops/clients?clientId=orbit-dashboard"
```

```json
[{"clientId": "orbit-dashboard", "rootUrl": "https://orbit-dash.example.com", "redirectUris": ["https://orbit-dash.example.com/*"], "publicClient": false}]
```

Any idea what's wrong? If it's easier to debug on a call, I'm reachable at pia.ops@example.com or
+1 555-0137 (platform team desk: 4 Example Plaza, Floor 3, Springfield).

comments.author: ines-v
