title: Postgres broker: ORB-1601 the first time a job result is written
body:
We just moved our Postgres-broker deployment from 2.9.0 to 3.0.3. Jobs run, but every job that
returns a value logs:

```text
2026-04-15T10:04:44Z ERROR orbit.results ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable: backend 'redis' requires a redis broker (broker is postgres)
```

We don't use Redis anywhere, and our `orbit.toml` only has `[broker]` and `[worker]`. Do we need
Redis for results now?
author: pg-wrangler

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
No Redis needed. The result backend defaults to `backend = "redis"` regardless of the broker, so
a Postgres deployment needs to say so explicitly:

```toml
[results]
backend = "postgres"
ttl_days = 7
```

Results and flow run records then go to tables (`orbit_results`, `orbit_flow_runs`) in the same
database as the broker, using the broker's connection. `orbit doctor` flags this mismatch before
you deploy, so it's worth running in CI. `results-backend` has the full table of backends.

comments.author: pg-wrangler
comments.body:
That fixed it. And yes, `orbit doctor` showed a ✘ for results, we just hadn't run it. Adding it to
CI now.

title: ORB-2001 IdempotencyConflict when the same job is enqueued positionally and by keyword
body:
Our checkout and our payment webhook can both enqueue the same charge. That's exactly what
`idempotency_key` is for, but one call site uses positional arguments:

```python
@app.job(idempotency_key="order_id", retries=5)
def charge(order_id: str, amount_cents: int): ...

charge.enqueue("A-1001", 1999)                        # checkout
charge.enqueue(order_id="A-1001", amount_cents=1999)  # webhook retry path
```

The second call raises even though the arguments are identical:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/payments/webhooks.py", line 61, in handle_payment_succeeded
    charge.enqueue(order_id=event.order_id, amount_cents=event.amount_cents)
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/job.py", line 236, in enqueue
    self._app.idempotency.claim(key, payload)
orbit.errors.IdempotencyConflict: ORB-2001 IdempotencyConflict: key 'A-1001' already used by job j_0c4d7e with different arguments
```

If both call sites use keywords, the second enqueue is de-duplicated as expected. We'd rather not
have a correctness feature depend on call style. orbit 3.0.3, Redis broker.
author: rubber-duck-rd

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Reproduced. Positional arguments are stored as a list and keyword arguments as a dict, and the
conflict check compares the stored payloads as-is, so the same call made two ways looks like
"different arguments". The check should normalise to keyword form before comparing. Marked S2
because it breaks de-duplication between call sites.

Workaround: use keyword arguments at every call site of jobs that have an `idempotency_key`. That's
the style `idempotency` uses in all its examples anyway.

comments.author: rubber-duck-rd
comments.body: Switched the checkout call to keywords. Works. Thanks for the quick diagnosis.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0: arguments are normalised to keyword form before the conflict check. Closing.

title: `--queues "default, high"` (space after comma) silently subscribes to a queue named " high"
body:
A teammate changed our worker command in a Helm chart to:

```bash
orbit worker --queues "default, high" --concurrency 8
```

Note the space after the comma. The worker started without complaint:

```text
2026-04-24T07:58:13Z INFO  orbit.worker  orbit 3.0.3 worker w-6d02 starting
2026-04-24T07:58:13Z INFO  orbit.worker  queues=default, high concurrency=8 prefetch=10
```

`high` jobs then sat in the queue for 40 minutes until someone noticed the dashboard flagging
`high` as "backlog, no consumers". The worker had subscribed to a queue literally named `" high"`.

Since queue names can't contain spaces, I'd expect the CLI to either strip whitespace or refuse to
start with an error.
author: maple-queue

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Agreed, this should never get as far as a running worker. Queue names may only contain lowercase
letters, digits, `-` and `_` (`concepts-queues-priorities`). The worker doesn't validate names it
subscribes to, and the space survives the split. Marking S2 because work silently stops being
processed.

The plan is to strip whitespace around each name *and* reject anything that's still invalid at
startup, so `--queues "default,Hi gh"` fails loudly instead of waiting forever. Until then, the
dashboard's "no consumers" flag is the best early warning.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0. Closing.

title: ORB-1102 WorkerHeartbeatLost during CPU-heavy jobs: is the worker broken?
body:
We have a forecasting job that does about three minutes of number crunching in pure Python
(lots of nested loops over dicts, no I/O). Whenever it runs, the other workers log a lost
heartbeat for the worker running it:

```text
2026-04-27T16:38:37Z INFO  orbit.worker  [w-9b2e] job j_c40e12 rebuild_forecast started (queue=analytics)
2026-04-27T16:40:12Z WARN  orbit.worker  [w-51aa] ORB-1102 WorkerHeartbeatLost: no heartbeat from w-9b2e for 95s (heartbeat_seconds=30)
2026-04-27T16:41:50Z INFO  orbit.worker  [w-9b2e] job j_c40e12 rebuild_forecast succeeded in 193.0s
```

The job always succeeds. Is this a problem, and should I raise `heartbeat_seconds`? orbit 3.0.3,
`concurrency = 2` on that worker.
author: paper-crane-dev

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
It is a problem, even though the job succeeds. Heartbeats are sent from a background thread in the
worker process. A long pure-Python loop holds the GIL for so long that the heartbeat thread rarely
gets to run, so the broker stops hearing from the worker. Two consequences:

- The other job slot on that worker can't renew its lease either.
- If the gap gets longer than `lease_seconds`, the job can be redelivered to another worker while
  this one is still running it.

Raising `heartbeat_seconds` makes it worse, not better. Options, in order of preference:

1. Run the heavy part in a subprocess (e.g. `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`) and wait on
   it from the job. The worker process stays responsive.
2. Split the job into smaller pieces, e.g. one job per forecast segment.
3. Give this job its own queue and a worker with `--concurrency 1`, so at least nothing else
   shares its process.

`concepts-workers` explains the worker anatomy, and `leases-and-heartbeats` covers how heartbeats
renew leases. ORB-1102 is in `error-codes` as well.

comments.author: paper-crane-dev
comments.body: Moved the crunching into a ProcessPoolExecutor. No more ORB-1102. Thanks for the explanation.

title: flow not working
body: my flow doesnt run the second step. what am i doing wrong
author: harbor-pilot

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Hard to say without more detail. Could you post the `Flow(...)` definition, the two job functions,
and the output of `orbit flows status <run_id>` for a run that didn't continue?

Common causes, in case one of them fits:

- the second step's `after=` doesn't match the first step's **name** exactly

- the second step expects an argument that's neither a run input nor an upstream step's name, so it

title: Retry delay exceeds [retries] max_delay_seconds when the job decorator sets backoff
body:
Global policy in `orbit.toml`:

```toml
[retries]
max_attempts = 3
backoff = "exponential"
max_delay_seconds = 600
```

One job needs more attempts:

```python
@app.job(retries=9, backoff="exponential", timeout="2m")
def sync_ledger(account_id: str): ...
```

Its later retries go well past the 600 s cap:

```text
2026-05-04T02:59:22Z WARN  orbit.retries job j_2f7781 attempt 5/9 failed, retrying in 320s
2026-05-04T03:10:02Z WARN  orbit.retries job j_2f7781 attempt 6/9 failed, retrying in 640s
2026-05-04T03:20:44Z WARN  orbit.retries job j_2f7781 attempt 7/9 failed, retrying in 1280s
```

Jobs that only use the global policy are capped correctly. I'd expect `max_delay_seconds` to apply
to every job unless the job overrides it. orbit 3.0.3.
author: copper-kite

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Confirmed. It's the same symptom as #23 on 2.8. The config loader was rewritten for `orbit.toml` in 3.0, and the per-job policy is again built from scratch when the decorator sets `backoff=`, so it doesn't inherit `max_delay_seconds` from `[retries]` and the delay keeps doubling. `retries=` alone is fine.

Workaround: drop `backoff="exponential"` from the decorator. It's the default, so you'll get the
same curve with the global cap. `retries-and-backoff` describes how per-job options are meant to
layer over `[retries]`.

comments.author: copper-kite
comments.body: Removing `backoff=` brings it back under 600 s. Thanks.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0: per-job policies now inherit any `[retries]` setting they don't override. Closing.

title: SQS: map Orbit queue names to existing, pre-provisioned SQS queues
body:
Our AWS accounts are locked down: every SQS queue is created by Terraform with a specific KMS key,
access policy, redrive settings and naming convention (`prod-billing-orbit-default`). The SQS broker
derives queue names from the Orbit queue name, so we have to bend our naming convention to match
Orbit's, and we can't use our existing queues.

**Request:** an optional mapping from Orbit queue name to an existing SQS queue URL or name, so
Orbit uses the queue as provisioned and never creates one. Without a mapping, keep today's
behaviour.
author: harbor-pilot

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Understood, and pretty common in locked-down accounts. `broker-sqs` documents the current naming
scheme. An explicit mapping is doable. The main thing to design is the DLQ, since Orbit manages its
own DLQ semantics on top of SQS and that needs to work with your redrive settings. Marking as a
feature request.

title: ScheduleParseError (ORB-1401) bei Wochentagsbereich MON-FRI
body:
Hallo zusammen,

mit Orbit 3.0.3 (Python 3.12.3) wird folgender Zeitplan beim Start abgelehnt:

```python
app.schedule(sync_lagerbestand, cron="30 6 * * MON-FRI")
```

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/lager/app/schedules.py", line 12, in <module>
    app.schedule(sync_lagerbestand, cron="30 6 * * MON-FRI")
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/scheduler/cron.py", line 88, in parse
    raise ScheduleParseError(...)
orbit.errors.ScheduleParseError: ORB-1401 ScheduleParseError: invalid day-of-week field 'MON-FRI' in '30 6 * * MON-FRI'
```

Einzelne Namen wie `MON` funktionieren (das Beispiel in der Doku nutzt `"0 9 * * MON"`), und der
numerische Bereich `1-5` funktioniert auch. Nur Bereiche mit Namen werden nicht akzeptiert. Laut
Standard-Cron-Syntax sollte `MON-FRI` gültig sein.

Wir nutzen vorerst `1-5`, aber das ist schlechter lesbar.

Viele Grüße
author: fernweh-ops

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Danke für den Bericht! (Answering in English.) Confirmed: the day-of-week parser accepts single
names and numeric ranges, but not ranges of names. That's a bug, since `MON-FRI` is standard cron
syntax. `1-5` is the right workaround in the meantime (Monday = 1). `scheduling-cron` will get an
example with a range once this is fixed.

comments.author: fernweh-ops
comments.body: Danke, wir bleiben bis zum Fix bei `1-5`.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0: named ranges like `MON-FRI` and lists like `MON,WED,FRI` are accepted. Closing.

title: How long are job results kept, and can I keep them for 30 days?
body:
Our support team looks up job results when customers complain ("did the export actually run?").
After about a week the result is gone and `handle.result()` for an old job id doesn't find it. Is
there a retention setting, and is there any downside to keeping results for 30 days? Redis
broker, default results config.
author: dev-ibis

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Retention is `[results] ttl_days`, 7 by default, counted from when the job (or flow run)
**finishes**:

```toml
[results]
backend = "redis"
ttl_days = 30
```

Flow runs that are still in progress never expire, whatever the TTL.

The downside is memory. On Redis, results live in the broker's database, so a rough estimate is
results per day × average result size × `ttl_days`. Going from 7 to 30 days roughly quadruples
it. Make sure Redis uses `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. With an evicting policy, Redis silently
deletes result keys and flow run records under pressure, which shows up as `ORB-1503` for flows.

If support only needs "did it run, and when?", consider writing that to your own database inside
the job instead. It's cheaper than keeping full results for a month. `results-backend` has the
sizing notes.

comments.author: dev-ibis
comments.body:
Our results are tiny, so 30 days is fine memory-wise. Set it and checked the eviction policy.
Thanks!

title: Every job logs a full ORB-1601 traceback while the result backend is unavailable (40k lines/min)
body:
Tonight a maintenance `VACUUM FULL` on our `orbit_results` table held a lock for ~25 minutes
(Postgres broker + Postgres result backend). Jobs kept running, as the docs say they should, but
every single job logged an ERROR with a full traceback when its result write timed out:

```text
2026-05-13T22:01:17Z ERROR orbit.results ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable: could not store result for job j_77ab10: canceling statement due to lock timeout
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/results/postgres.py", line 91, in store
    cur.execute(INSERT_RESULT, params)
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/psycopg/cursor.py", line 732, in execute
    raise ex.with_traceback(None)
psycopg.errors.LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout
2026-05-13T22:01:17Z ERROR orbit.results ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable: could not store result for job j_77ab13: canceling statement due to lock timeout
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
```

That's ~40,000 log lines per minute across our workers, which tripped our log pipeline's rate limit
and dropped logs from *other* services. The VACUUM was our mistake, but a single outage of the
result backend shouldn't produce one traceback per job.

**Expected:** log the first failure with a traceback, then a periodic summary (e.g. "ORB-1601: 1,532
result writes failed in the last 60s") until it recovers.
author: dev-ibis

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Agreed. A dependency outage should produce a handful of lines, not one per job. We'll log the
first occurrence in full and then a rate-limited summary with a count, plus a recovery line when
writes succeed again. The ORB-1601 counter metric is unaffected, so alert on that rather than log
volume (`observability-metrics`).

Side note for anyone finding this later: during an ORB-1601 outage the jobs still run, but their
results and flow state aren't saved. `results-backend` covers what that means for flows.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0. Closing.

title: Jobs delayed by ~5 seconds after putting PgBouncer in front of the Postgres broker
body:
We introduced PgBouncer (transaction pooling) between our workers and Postgres to cut connection
count. Since then, job pickup latency went from ~100 ms to a steady 4-5 seconds. No
errors, nothing in the DLQ, jobs do eventually run. Rolling the workers back to direct connections
fixes it. orbit 3.0.3, Postgres 16, PgBouncer 1.22.
author: tundra-ops

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
`LISTEN` is session-scoped, so it doesn't work through PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. The
listener connection gets returned to the pool and the worker never receives notifications. It
then only finds jobs on its periodic poll, the fixed 5-second safety-net poll, which matches your 4-5 s.

Connect workers directly, or use a separate PgBouncer pool in **session** mode for workers.
`troubleshooting-broker` has this under "Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY misses events under load".

comments.author: tundra-ops
comments.body: Session pooling for workers brought p50 back to ~100 ms. p99 still spikes to ~5 s during our hourly bulk enqueue, though, even with session pooling.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
That remaining spike under bulk load is #87, which we're still investigating. Closing this as a
duplicate so it's all in one place. Please add your bulk-enqueue numbers there.

title: Cancel a running flow run
body:
Sometimes we start a big backfill flow with the wrong inputs and want to stop it. There's no way
to do that today. The closest thing is waiting for a step to fail and purging its DLQ entry, which
leaves the run `failed`, but a run whose steps keep succeeding just carries on.

**Request:** `orbit flows cancel <run_id>` (and the same from Python / the dashboard) that:

- stops enqueuing further steps,
- marks queued/pending steps as cancelled,
- lets currently running steps finish (or optionally interrupts them),
- leaves the run in a distinct `cancelled` state rather than `failed`.
author: cron-jules

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Reasonable, and it overlaps with #81 (cancelling a queued job). Cancelling the *queued* parts of a
run is the easy half, since the run record already knows which steps are pending or queued.
Interrupting running steps is harder and would probably reuse the timeout mechanism.

For now the workaround is to deploy a guard in the step functions that checks a flag and returns
early. `flows-error-handling` describes how purging DLQ entries affects a run. Keeping this open as
a feature request.

title: `orbit dlq list` shows ATTEMPTS 1 for jobs that were retried 5 times
body:
Our SMS reminder job is configured with `retries=5`. The worker log clearly shows five attempts
before the job is dead-lettered:

```text
2026-05-20T06:12:44Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted: job j_93c1aa moved to DLQ after 5 attempts
```

But `orbit dlq list` reports a single attempt for every entry:

```text
$ orbit dlq list
JOB ID     QUEUE  JOB                ATTEMPTS  FAILED AT             ERROR
j_93c1aa   sms    send_reminder_sms  1         2026-05-20T06:12:44Z  SmsGatewayTimeout
j_93c1b4   sms    send_reminder_sms  1         2026-05-20T06:12:51Z  SmsGatewayTimeout
j_93c1c9   sms    send_reminder_sms  1         2026-05-20T06:13:02Z  SmsGatewayTimeout
```

The dashboard's job detail page has the same wrong count. Here's what it shows for the first
entry:

```json
{"id": "j_93c1aa", "job": "send_reminder_sms", "attempts": 1, "args": {"customer_id": "c_5512", "phone": "+1 555-0188", "email": "m.alvarez@example.com", "address": "221 Example Lane, Apt 4, Springfield"}}
```

This made our on-call think retries were broken. orbit 3.0.3, Redis broker.

— Quill, support engineering (escalations: oncall-support@example.com, +1 555-0163)
author: quillfeather

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Thanks, reproduced. The DLQ entry records the attempt number of the delivery that dead-lettered
it (`1` after the last retry is re-enqueued) instead of the job's total attempt count. The retries
themselves happen correctly, as your log shows, so this is a display bug in the CLI and dashboard.

Unrelated but worth flagging: that job's arguments include a phone number, email and street
address. Those values now sit in the broker, the DLQ and the dashboard for as long as the entry
lives. `security` recommends passing an id (`customer_id`) and looking up contact details inside
the job. I'd also suggest editing the issue to remove the customer record and your escalation
contacts.

comments.author: quillfeather
comments.body: Good point on the arguments. These are test customers, but we'll switch to passing only the id.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.0: `orbit dlq list` and the dashboard show the total number of attempts. Closing.

title: error when starting worker
body: getting an error when I start the worker. any ideas?
author: kiwi-in-prod

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
We'll need the error itself, plus your Orbit version and how you start the worker (command, Docker,
Kubernetes...). The first line containing an `ORB-` code is usually the most useful.

comments.author: kiwi-in-prod
comments.body:
sorry. 3.0.3 in docker. it keeps printing this:

```text
WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to localhost:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 7)
```

but our redis is not on localhost, it's in the orbit.toml as redis://cache.internal.example.com:6379/0

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
`localhost:6379` is the default broker, which suggests the worker isn't finding your `orbit.toml`
at all. It looks in the working directory. Check the `WORKDIR` of the image against where the file
is copied, then run `orbit doctor` in the container. The second line of its output shows which
config file it loaded. `deployment-docker` has a reference Dockerfile.

comments.author: kiwi-in-prod
comments.body: yep, WORKDIR was /srv but the file was in /app. works now, thanks

title: api-reference-job: the handle returned by enqueue() isn't documented
body:
`api-reference-job` documents `@app.job(...)` options and `.enqueue(...)` arguments, but not what
`enqueue()` returns. I only found `handle.id` and `handle.result(timeout=...)` by reading
`results-backend`. It would help to have the handle's attributes and methods on the API reference
page, including what `.result()` raises when the job failed or timed out.
author: pg-wrangler

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Good catch. I've drafted a section for `api-reference-job` covering the handle: `id`,
`result(timeout=...)`, and the three outcomes (return value, the job's last exception re-raised
after `ORB-1301`, or `TimeoutError` while the job keeps running). It'll go live with the next docs
deploy.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Published. Closing.

title: glossary: "lease" and "visibility timeout" are used interchangeably on the SQS page
body:
`broker-sqs` switches between "lease" and "visibility timeout" within the same section, and
`glossary` only defines "lease". Are these the same thing? If so, which setting controls it on SQS:
`[worker] lease_seconds`, or the queue's visibility timeout configured in AWS?
author: tidepool-io

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Same concept: "lease" is Orbit's generic term, and on SQS it's implemented with the message's
visibility timeout. Orbit sets it from `[worker] lease_seconds` when it receives a message and
extends it on each heartbeat (that's why the worker role needs `sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility`), so
the queue-level default in AWS doesn't matter for Orbit's jobs.

I've added "visibility timeout" to `glossary` as a synonym pointing to "lease", and made
`broker-sqs` use "lease (visibility timeout)" on first mention and "lease" after that. Closing.

title: `orbit dlq replay` re-enqueues a high-priority job as normal priority
body:
Password-reset emails are enqueued with `priority="high"`. After an outage at our email provider we
replayed the DLQ entries:

```text
$ orbit dlq replay j_4410ce
replayed j_4410ce -> j_4419f2
```

In the dashboard the new job `j_4419f2` has priority `normal`, so the replayed resets queued behind
~30k normal-priority newsletter jobs and took 20 minutes to go out. I'd expect a replay to keep the
priority (and any queue override) of the original enqueue.

orbit 3.0.3.
author: vantablack-v

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Confirmed. Replay builds the new job from the job's decorator defaults and drops the per-enqueue
options, so `priority` and a `queue=` override at enqueue time are both lost. That's a bug. The DLQ
entry has the original options, replay just doesn't use them.

Workaround for urgent replays: re-enqueue from a Python shell with the right options and then
`orbit dlq purge` once you're sure everything is back. Note that `purge` clears every DLQ entry,
so it's only an option if nothing else in there needs keeping. `dead-letter-queue` describes
replay and purge.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.2: replay preserves the original priority and queue. Closing.

title: idempotency_key based on two arguments (tenant_id + invoice_id)?
body:
In our multi-tenant app invoice numbers are only unique per tenant:

```python
@app.job(retries=3)
def deliver_invoice(tenant_id: str, invoice_id: str): ...
```

`idempotency_key` takes the *name of one argument*. If I use `idempotency_key="invoice_id"`, two
tenants with invoice `INV-1001` would collide. Would the second one fail with ORB-2001
IdempotencyConflict? What's the recommended way to key on both?
author: cobalt-wren

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Yes. Same key with different arguments raises `ORB-2001 IdempotencyConflict`, so keying on
`invoice_id` alone would reject the second tenant's job. Add an explicit key argument built from
everything that makes the work unique:

```python
@app.job(retries=3, idempotency_key="delivery_key")
def deliver_invoice(tenant_id: str, invoice_id: str, delivery_key: str): ...

deliver_invoice.enqueue(
    tenant_id="t_204", invoice_id="INV-1001", delivery_key="t_204:INV-1001"
)
```

The job can ignore `delivery_key` in its body. `idempotency` shows this composite-key pattern,
and the ORB-2001 entry in `error-codes` has the same advice.

comments.author: cobalt-wren
comments.body: Composite key it is. Thanks.

title: SQS: ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError message doesn't say which IAM action was denied
body:
After a security team tightened our IAM policies, workers started logging:

```text
2026-05-30T12:44:09Z ERROR orbit.broker.sqs ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError: access denied
```

That's the whole message. It took us an hour in CloudTrail to find that the denied call was
`sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility` (heartbeats), while receive and delete were still allowed. botocore's
exception has the error code and the operation name, so Orbit seems to drop them when wrapping it.

Could the message include the AWS error code, the operation and the queue, e.g.
`access denied: AccessDenied on ChangeMessageVisibility (queue prod-orders-default)`?
author: harbor-node

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Yes, we wrap the botocore `ClientError` and keep only a generic message. That's an easy fix and
we'll include the error code, operation and queue name. The auth section of `troubleshooting-broker`
lists every permission the SQS broker needs (`sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `sqs:DeleteMessage`,
`sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility` and `sqs:SendMessage`). Worth sharing with your security team.
3.1.0 is already frozen, so this will land in the next patch.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Shipped in 3.1.2. Closing.

title: ORB-1503 FlowStateCorrupt for in-flight runs during a rolling upgrade from 3.0.3 to 3.1.0
body:
We upgraded our statement workers from 3.0.3 to 3.1.0 with a normal Kubernetes rolling update
(25% max unavailable). While old and new pods were both running, 14 in-flight flow runs failed:

```text
2026-06-02T09:15:33Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1503 FlowStateCorrupt: run record fr_01JWD4K7NB could not be decoded
2026-06-02T09:15:41Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1503 FlowStateCorrupt: run record fr_01JWD4M1TA could not be decoded
```

Once all pods were on 3.1.0, new runs worked fine. Redis is configured with `noeviction` and
nobody touched the keys. Is this expected when mixing versions, and how should we upgrade flow
workers next time?
author: ochre-moth

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Yes, mixed versions are one of the documented causes of ORB-1503: a worker can fail to read a run
record that a different version wrote, or the other way round. Plain jobs don't have this problem,
because they don't share a run record. That's why only your flows were affected.

For flow workers, avoid having two versions process the same runs:

- stop starting new runs, let in-flight runs finish (watch `orbit flows status` or the dashboard),
  then upgrade all flow workers at once, or
- use a `Recreate` strategy for the deployment that serves your flow queues, and accept a short
  pause.

The affected runs can't be resumed. Start new runs for them and purge their DLQ entries so nobody
replays into a broken run. `flows-steps-and-state` has the "Protecting run state" section, and
`flows-error-handling` covers recovering from ORB-1503.

comments.author: ochre-moth
comments.body: Thanks. We'll drain and recreate for the flow pool from now on. Re-ran the 14 statements.

title: 3.1.0: reconnect storm after Redis failover, thousands of connections and an ORB-1001 flood take Redis down again
body:
**Production outage, 47 minutes.** We upgraded to 3.1.0 on Monday. Last night our managed Redis
did a routine primary failover (replica promoted, DNS updated). On 3.0.3 the same failover drills
were a non-event: a few ORB-1001 warnings, then workers reconnected.

With 3.1.0, every worker slot started reconnecting at once with no backoff. Note the attempt
counter never goes above 1:

```text
2026-06-03T02:00:14Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-06-03T02:00:14Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-06-03T02:00:14Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
... repeated ~4,000 times in the first 20 seconds
2026-06-03T02:00:35Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-primary.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 1)
2026-06-03T02:00:35Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-primary.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 1)
```

Redis metrics during the incident:

| Time (UTC) | `connected_clients` | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| 01:59 | 680 | 18% |
| 02:00:30 | 9,412 | 100% |
| 02:03 | (second failover, new primary unresponsive) | 100% |
| 02:47 | 640 after scaling workers to 0 and back up in batches | 22% |

Setup: 40 worker pods × `--concurrency 16`, Redis 7.2, `orbit[redis]` 3.1.0, Python 3.12.3.

We had to scale every worker deployment to zero to let Redis recover. We've pinned 3.0.3 again for
now.
author: cron-jules

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Thank you for the timeline and the metrics, and sorry for the outage. Confirmed as a regression in
3.1.0. The connection handling was reworked, and after a failover each worker *slot* now
reconnects independently and immediately instead of sharing one reconnect with backoff per worker
process. With 640 slots that's thousands of simultaneous connections against a freshly promoted
primary. Marked S1.

Until there's a fix:

- **Pinning 3.0.3 is the safest option**, as you've done.
- If you have to stay on 3.1.0: during a failover, stop all workers, wait for it to finish, then
  start workers in small batches.
- A Redis `maxclients` limit protects the broker from falling over again, but not your throughput.

Write-up in `troubleshooting-broker` under "Redis reconnect storm after failover (3.1.0)".

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Fix is in review: reconnects use jittered exponential backoff again, and each worker process makes
a single reconnect attempt that all its slots wait on. We're targeting 3.1.2. We'll also add a
failover drill to the release checklist so this can't regress silently again.

comments.author: cron-jules
comments.body:
Thanks both. We'll stay on 3.0.3 until 3.1.2 and run our failover drill against it before rolling
out.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
3.1.2 is out with the fix (see `changelog`). In our drill with 800 slots, a failover now peaks at
about one connection per worker process and recovers in under 10 seconds. Closing. Please reopen
if you see anything different in your drill.

title: ORB-1702 at dashboard startup when oidc_issuer has a trailing slash
body:
Our Helm chart builds `oidc_issuer` from a base URL and ends up with a trailing slash. On 3.1.0
the dashboard refuses to start:

```text
2026-06-05T07:30:12Z ERROR orbit.dashboard ORB-1702 OIDCMisconfigured: issuer mismatch: configured 'https://login.example.com/auth/realms/ops/' but discovery document says 'https://login.example.com/auth/realms/ops'
```

Removing the slash fixes it. I know OIDC says the issuer must match exactly, but the error only
says "mismatch", and the two strings look identical at a glance in a narrow terminal. Could Orbit
normalise a trailing slash, or at least point out that the only difference is the slash?
author: patchwork-pia

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Fair. The comparison is exact on purpose, since the `iss` claim in tokens has to match too. But a
trailing slash is by far the most common way people trip over this. We'll normalise a trailing slash
on the configured value before fetching discovery, and when the comparison still fails, the message
will show which part differs. `dashboard-auth-oidc` will get a note in its ORB-1702 checklist.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Shipped in 3.1.2. Closing.

title: Redis CPU pegged at 100% after Sentinel failover; workers never recover
body:
Sentinel failed over our Redis primary at 06:12 this morning (orbit 3.1.0). Since then the new
primary sits at 100% CPU and the workers are stuck in a loop of:

2026-06-08T06:12:09Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)

`CLIENT LIST` shows about 6,000 connections from our 24 worker hosts. No jobs are being processed.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
This is the 3.1.0 reconnect storm tracked in #143. To recover now: stop **all** workers, wait until

comments.author: zinc-zebra
comments.body: Stopping everything and starting in batches of 4 worked. Back on 3.0.3. Thanks.

title: `orbit doctor`: machine-readable output for CI
body:
We run `orbit doctor` as a deploy gate. Its output is great for humans, but for CI we'd like to
know *which* check failed without scraping ✔/✘ lines, e.g. to retry only broker reachability
checks and fail fast on config errors.

**Request:** a JSON output mode, e.g. one object per check with `name`, `ok`, `message` and the ORB
code when there is one. A documented exit-code contract would be nice too.
author: lumen-dev

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Sounds good, and it's the same ask as #92 (JSON output for `orbit dlq list`), so we'll make the CLI
consistent across commands. On exit codes: `doctor` exits non-zero if any check fails, as
`installation` documents. A finer contract (e.g. different codes for config vs. connectivity)
would fit well with the JSON mode. Marking as a feature request.

title: 3.1.0: `orbit doctor` prints a failed results check but still says "All checks passed" and exits 0
body:
After #120 we added `orbit doctor` to CI. A new service was deployed with the result backend
misconfigured, and CI didn't catch it:

```text
$ orbit doctor; echo "exit=$?"
✔ orbit 3.1.0, python 3.11.9
✔ config: ./orbit.toml (4 sections, 0 unknown keys)
✔ broker: postgres://orbit_worker@pg.internal.example.com:5432/jobs reachable (postgres 16.2, 2.3 ms)
✘ results: ORB-1601 ResultBackendUnavailable: backend 'redis' requires a redis broker (broker is postgres)
✔ worker: heartbeat_seconds (30) <= lease_seconds (300) / 3
All checks passed.
exit=0
```

On 3.0.3 the same misconfiguration printed `1 check failed.` and exited 1.
author: pg-wrangler

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Confirmed, a 3.1.0 regression. The results check was rewritten to report problems as a result
instead of raising, and the summary only counts checks that raised. So you get the ✘ line but a
green summary and exit 0. That defeats the point of running it in CI.

Workaround until the fix: fail the CI step if the output contains `✘`, e.g.
`orbit doctor | tee doctor.txt; ! grep -q '✘' doctor.txt`. And for this service, set
`[results] backend = "postgres"` (`results-backend`).

comments.author: pg-wrangler
comments.body: Added the grep to our pipeline. Thanks.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Fixed in 3.1.2, along with a test that any ✘ line means a non-zero exit. Closing.

title: Nightly report flow fails with ORB-1202 since data volume grew
body:
Our `nightly-report` flow worked for months. Since the start of June the `aggregate` step fails
every night:

```text
2026-06-11T01:22:10Z ERROR orbit.flows   ORB-1202 PayloadTooLarge: result of step 'aggregate' is 611 KB (max_payload_kb=512)
2026-06-11T01:41:52Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted: job j_e0a7d3 moved to DLQ after 3 attempts
```

The step returns a dict of per-region totals that has grown past 512 KB. Each retry recomputes
everything (~6 minutes) and fails the same way. Is the fix just to raise `max_payload_kb`?
author: mossy-stack

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Raising `max_payload_kb` would get you through tonight, but the totals will keep growing, and the
limit applies to every payload in the deployment (`performance-tuning` explains why that's rarely
the right fix). Better: write the totals to storage in `aggregate` and return a reference, as shown
in `flows-steps-and-state`.

The repeated retries on a deterministic ORB-1202 are tracked in #102. Closing this as a duplicate
of that issue.

title: Worker OOM-killed by Kubernetes shows up as ORB-1102 heartbeat lost, not ORB-2101 WorkerOOM
body:
One of our worker pods hit its memory limit and was OOM-killed by Kubernetes:

```text
$ kubectl get pod reports-worker-7d9f-xk2lp -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}'
OOMKilled
```

Orbit's side of the story only shows a lost heartbeat:

```text
2026-06-12T04:22:51Z WARN  orbit.worker  [w-51aa] ORB-1102 WorkerHeartbeatLost: no heartbeat from w-3e07 for 92s (heartbeat_seconds=30)
```

The dashboard lists `w-3e07` as "heartbeat lost", and our alert on ORB-2101 WorkerOOM never fired.
We only noticed because the jobs were redelivered after their leases expired. I expected ORB-2101
here. Is WorkerOOM only reported in some situations?
author: dev-ibis

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
ORB-2101 is reported when the worker process itself sees a job process being killed for memory.
When the kernel kills the whole container, nothing is left running to report it, so from the
broker's point of view the worker's heartbeats just stop, and that's ORB-1102.

That's explainable, but it's not a great experience. Knowing *why* a worker disappeared matters
for on-call. Ideas we're looking at: have the replacement worker report the previous instance's
exit reason when it's available, and surface "possibly OOM-killed" in the dashboard's worker view.
Keeping this open. Meanwhile, alert on ORB-1102 as well, and on the container's OOMKilled reason
from Kubernetes. `troubleshooting-memory` covers finding what's using the memory.

title: ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError spam after Redis primary switch on 3.1.0
body:
After our Redis primary was switched over this morning, workers logged ~25,000 lines of

```text
2026-06-15T08:31:02Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
```

in about two minutes, and job throughput dropped to near zero for ~10 minutes before recovering by
itself. We have a small setup (6 workers × concurrency 4), so Redis survived, but it looks wrong
that every log line says "attempt 1". orbit 3.1.0.
author: neon-newt

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
That's the 3.1.0 reconnect storm (#143): after a failover every worker slot reconnects at once,
with no backoff. Smaller deployments usually recover on their own like yours did. Larger ones can
knock Redis over. The fix is coming in 3.1.2. Until then, pinning 3.0.3 avoids it.
`troubleshooting-broker` has the workaround. Closing as a duplicate of #143.

title: Per-job result retention instead of one global ttl_days
body:
Follow-up to #131. We raised `[results] ttl_days` to 30 for the support team, but that only matters
for two job types (exports and invoice deliveries). Everything else, including high-volume jobs
whose results nobody reads, is now also kept for 30 days.

**Request:** let a job override the retention of its own results, something like a
`result_ttl_days` option on `@app.job`, with `[results] ttl_days` as the default. A way to not store
the result at all for a given job would be useful too.
author: dev-ibis

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Makes sense. Retention is global today (`results-backend`, "Retention"), and per-job overrides
would cut result storage a lot for setups like yours. Flow runs complicate it a bit, since their
records outlive the step results inside them, so the first version would probably cover plain
jobs only. Marking as a feature request.

title: Is idempotency_key enforced on SQS standard queues? Docs unclear
body:
`troubleshooting-broker` suggests switching from FIFO to a standard queue "and make jobs safe to
run twice with an `idempotency_key`". But neither `idempotency` nor `broker-sqs` explains how the
key behaves on SQS. Is it checked at enqueue like on Redis? What happens on redelivery? Please
document this. It's the one thing blocking our move off FIFO.
author: patchwork-pia

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Sorry this is still missing. It's tracked in #94, so I'm closing this as a duplicate and bumping
that one. The page is next on my list. The short version: Orbit's `idempotency_key` doesn't depend
on FIFO deduplication, which is why the troubleshooting page recommends it for standard queues.
The SQS-specific details are what #94 will add.

title: Dashboard DLQ: "Replay selected" replays every entry matching the filter, not just the selected ones
body:
Steps (3.1.0):

1. Open the DLQ page and filter by job `sync_ledger` (340 entries).
2. Tick the checkboxes of **two** entries.
3. Click "Replay selected" and confirm.

All 340 `sync_ledger` entries were replayed, including ones we deliberately wanted to keep in the
DLQ because their accounts are being investigated. The confirmation dialog said "Replay 2 jobs?".

That's a fairly dangerous mismatch for a button on an admin tool.
author: mossy-stack

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Confirmed, and agreed it's serious: the dialog counts the selection, but the request sends the
current filter instead of the selected ids. Marked S2.

Until the fix ships, please replay individual entries from the CLI with `orbit dlq replay <job_id>`,
or use the per-row "Replay" action, which isn't affected. `dead-letter-queue` covers replay in
general. Replaying a job runs it again, so the jobs you wanted to hold back may need a manual
look.

comments.author: mossy-stack
comments.body: Thanks. Luckily the ledger syncs are idempotent, so the extra replays were harmless this time.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Fixed in 3.1.2: bulk replay sends exactly the selected ids, and the confirmation lists them.
Closing.

title: Pause and resume a schedule without a deploy
body:
Schedules are declared in code with `app.schedule(...)`, so stopping one temporarily (say, the
nightly partner sync while the partner is down) means a code change and a deploy, then another
deploy to turn it back on.

**Request:** a way to pause and resume a schedule at runtime, from the CLI or the dashboard. While
paused, runs are skipped (not queued up and fired all at once on resume). The dashboard should show
paused schedules clearly.
author: rubber-duck-rd

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
Common request, and a good one. The main design question is what "paused" means across a deploy:
the schedule definition still comes from code, so the pause state needs to live in the broker and
survive restarts. Skipping (rather than catching up) on resume is the behaviour we'd want too.
`scheduling-cron` describes how schedules are registered today. Marking as a feature request.

title: retries not working after upgrade to 3.1?
body: since upgrading to 3.1 it feels like retries dont happen anymore. is this a known thing?
author: tundra-ops

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Nothing like that is known for 3.1.0, so we need a few details to dig in:

- the `@app.job(...)` decorator of an affected job
- the `[retries]` section of your `orbit.toml` (or tell us if there isn't one)
- worker log lines for one failing job. Retries log `attempt N/M failed, retrying in ...`, and the
  final failure logs `ORB-1301 RetryExhausted`
- which version you upgraded from, and whether you changed config as part of the upgrade

`retries-and-backoff` describes how the decorator options and `[retries]` combine.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Closing since we haven't heard back. Reopen with the details above if this is still happening.

title: deployment-kubernetes: clarify whether the `orbit doctor` probe is for liveness or readiness
body:
The Kubernetes example runs `orbit doctor` in an exec probe but doesn't say which kind of probe it's
meant for. We copied it as a **liveness** probe. During a 40-second broker blip yesterday, every
worker pod failed the probe and was restarted at the same moment, which turned a short blip into a
much longer recovery.

Could the page say explicitly that `orbit doctor` belongs in readiness/startup probes, and suggest
something for liveness that doesn't depend on the broker being up?
author: tundra-ops

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Thanks, that's an important clarification. `orbit doctor` checks the broker, so it's a readiness
(or startup) probe. `installation` calls it a readiness step, but `deployment-kubernetes` didn't say
so. A liveness probe that depends on an external system restarts everything at once during an
outage, exactly as you saw. Workers already retry the broker connection with backoff on their own
and don't exit.

I've updated `deployment-kubernetes`: the example is labelled `readinessProbe`, there's a warning
against using it for liveness, and the liveness probe now only checks that the worker process
responds. Closing.

title: Jobs silently disappear on managed Redis: never run, never reach the DLQ
body:
Since we moved the Orbit broker to a managed Redis two weeks ago, a small number of jobs vanish. `.enqueue()` returns a handle, but the job never runs, it isn't in `orbit dlq list`, and the dashboard has never heard of its ID. We only noticed because a nightly reconciliation found about 300 orders a day with no receipt sent.

Nothing in the worker or producer logs. On the Redis side:

```text
$ redis-cli -h redis.internal.example.com INFO stats | grep evicted
evicted_keys:18342
$ redis-cli -h redis.internal.example.com CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
1) "maxmemory-policy"
2) "volatile-lru"
```

Memory sits near the instance limit during the evening batch, partly because we keep results for 14 days (`[results] ttl_days = 14`). Is Orbit supposed to cope with eviction, or is this a bug in the broker?

Orbit 3.1.0, Python 3.12.3, Redis 7.2 (managed).
author: rubber-duck-rd

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
It's the eviction policy rather than a bug in the broker. Redis is deleting Orbit's keys under memory pressure. A job whose hash has been evicted can't be claimed, retried or dead-lettered, so it disappears without a trace, exactly as you describe. Orbit needs `noeviction` (see "Required Redis settings" in `broker-redis`):

```conf
maxmemory-policy noeviction
```

With `noeviction`, a full Redis makes enqueues fail loudly instead, which you can alert on. Two more things:

- `orbit doctor` warns when the policy is anything other than `noeviction`. Run it in CI against the managed instance, because managed services often default to `volatile-lru`.
- Results live in the broker's database, so 14 days of results is eating the memory your queues need. Lower `[results] ttl_days` or size the instance for it (`results-backend` has the formula).

The evicted jobs are gone from Redis. Your reconciliation is the right way to re-enqueue them.

comments.author: rubber-duck-rd
comments.body: `orbit doctor` did warn about it, we just never ran it against prod. Policy is `noeviction` now, `ttl_days` is back to 7, and the reconciliation re-enqueued yesterday's orders. Thanks.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Glad it's sorted. Closing as a configuration issue.

title: Is it safe to raise max_payload_kb to 4096 for jobs that carry PDFs?
body:
Our document-ingest job receives the PDF as a base64 string argument. Larger documents fail at
enqueue time:

```text
orbit.errors.PayloadTooLarge: ORB-1202 PayloadTooLarge: payload for job 'ingest_document' is 1,184 KB (max_payload_kb=512)
```

Is there any problem with just setting `[limits] max_payload_kb = 4096`? Most PDFs are under 1 MB,
a few are around 3 MB. Redis broker, orbit 3.1.0.
author: kiwi-in-prod

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
You *can*, but we'd advise against it. The limit applies to every payload in the deployment, and
big payloads make every broker round trip slower. They also sit in Redis memory for as long as the
job is queued, delayed or in the DLQ, and they show up in the dashboard. `performance-tuning` puts it
bluntly: raising `max_payload_kb` is almost never the right fix for ORB-1202. `security` also points
out that the limit is your first defence against something flooding the broker with huge payloads.

The standard pattern is to upload the PDF to object storage first and pass the key:

```python
key = blob_store.put(f"ingest/{doc_id}.pdf", pdf_bytes)
ingest_document.enqueue(doc_id=doc_id, blob_key=key)
```

That keeps the payload to a few hundred bytes whatever the document size.

comments.author: kiwi-in-prod
comments.body: Makes sense. We already have a bucket for the originals, so we'll pass the key. Thanks.

title: `orbit dlq list` columns are misaligned when job names are long

title: Dashboard: search jobs by idempotency key
body:
When a customer says "my order was charged twice", the first thing we want to know is which jobs
exist for that order. Our charge job uses `idempotency_key="order_id"`, so the order id is exactly
the right handle, but the dashboard can only search by job id.

**Request:** a search box (or filter) on the jobs and DLQ pages that finds jobs by idempotency key
value, showing every attempt and its state.
author: saffron-ops

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Good idea, and a natural fit for incident work. The key value is already stored with the job, so it
mostly needs indexing per broker. One caution we'd put in the docs: if your keys contain personal
data (an email, say), searching by them puts that data in URLs and access logs. Ids like `order_id`
are the right kind of key (`idempotency`). Marking as a feature request.

title: Redis failover causes reconnect storm: thousands of connections and ORB-1001 for ~14 minutes
body:
We did a planned failover of our managed Redis (primary/replica behind a failover endpoint) last night and the whole Orbit fleet went sideways for about 14 minutes, long after the new primary was healthy.

**Setup**
- Orbit 3.1.0, Python 3.12.4
- 40 worker pods, each `orbit worker --queues default,high --concurrency 16`
- Redis 7.2, `maxclients 10000`
- Broker URL is the failover endpoint, e.g. `redis://orbit-redis.internal.example.com:6379/0`

Normal steady state is ~720 client connections (40 × (16 + 2), which matches the sizing note in the docs). During the failover `connected_clients` went to 9,987 and Redis CPU sat at 100%. New connections were refused with `max number of clients reached`, which made workers retry even harder.

```text
2026-06-30T22:03:11Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:11Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:11Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:12Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to orbit-redis.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:12Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to orbit-redis.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:19Z INFO  orbit.broker.redis connected to orbit-redis.internal.example.com:6379 (role=master)
2026-06-30T22:03:19Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:19Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:03:19Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 1)
...
2026-06-30T22:16:52Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 1)
2026-06-30T22:17:05Z INFO  orbit.worker resumed claiming on queues=default,high
```

The attempts all land within the same second on every pod. As far as I can tell there is no jitter at all, and every slot seems to reconnect on its own, not once per process.

We only got out of it by scaling the deployment to 0 and back up in batches of 5. Is there a supported way to make reconnects back off? We fail over once a quarter for patching, so this will happen again.
author: dk-cloud

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Thanks for the very complete report, and sorry you hit this. It's the 3.1.0 reconnect storm tracked in #143. The connection manager in 3.1.0 reconnects **per slot** with no jitter, so after a failover every slot on every process retries at the same moment, and every refused connection starts over. Your numbers (40 pods × 16 slots, `connected_clients` at the cap within seconds) match what we saw in our own drill.

The fix (full-jitter exponential backoff, plus one shared reconnect per process instead of one per slot) is merged and ships in **3.1.2**, planned for next week.

Until then, the mitigations in `broker-redis` ("Failover and high availability") apply:

- pin 3.0.3, which doesn't have the regression
- after a failover, stop all workers and start them again in small batches, and lower `--concurrency` temporarily (fewer slots, fewer pooled connections per process)

If you have another planned failover before the release, scale down to a handful of workers first. Closing as a duplicate of #143. Please follow that issue for the release.

comments.author: dk-cloud
comments.body: Thanks. We'll hold the next patch window until 3.1.2 lands and run a failover drill against it first.

title: Fan-out then fan-in in a Flow: how does the last step get both results?
body:
I'm moving an order pipeline from hand-rolled chained jobs to Flows (3.1.0). The shape is:

```
reserve_stock -> charge_card -> print_label  \
                             -> send_receipt -> close_order
```

`print_label` and `send_receipt` can run in parallel after `charge_card`, and `close_order` must wait for both. I have this so far:

```python
fulfil = Flow("fulfil-order", steps=[
    step(reserve_stock),
    step(charge_card, after="reserve_stock"),
    step(print_label, after="charge_card"),
    step(send_receipt, after="charge_card"),
    step(close_order, after="send_receipt"),
])
```

Two questions:
1. How do I make `close_order` wait for *both* branches? Do I need a dummy join step?
2. `close_order` needs the tracking number returned by `print_label`. How do I get it in there? I don't see anything like a `context` object.
author: hollis-sre

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
No dummy step needed.

1. `after=` accepts a list: `step(close_order, after=["print_label", "send_receipt"])`. The step is enqueued once every listed parent has succeeded.
2. Results are injected **by parameter name**. If `close_order` has a parameter called `print_label`, Orbit passes in the return value of the `print_label` step:

```python
@app.job()
def close_order(order_id: str, print_label: dict) -> None:
    tracking = print_label["tracking_number"]
    ...
```

`order_id` comes from the run inputs (`fulfil.run(order_id="A-1001")`). One gotcha: you can only inject results from steps in your own `after` chain, not from siblings. Both points are covered in `flows-steps-and-state` ("Passing data between steps").

comments.author: hollis-sre
comments.body: That's much nicer than what I was about to build. Works, thanks!

title: `orbit dlq replay`: accept several job IDs (or read them from stdin)
body:
**Problem**

We have ~3,000 entries in the DLQ after a downstream outage and I want to replay only the `sync_invoices` jobs. Following "Replaying many jobs" in `dead-letter-queue`, I'm doing this:

```bash
orbit dlq list | awk 'NR>1 && $2 == "sync_invoices" {print $1}' | xargs -n1 orbit dlq replay
```

It works, but `xargs -n1` starts one `orbit` process per ID, and each one loads the config and opens a broker connection to replay a single job. For ~1,900 jobs it took over 25 minutes.

**Request**

- `orbit dlq replay` accepting several job IDs: `orbit dlq replay j_1 j_2 j_3`
- and/or reading IDs from stdin: `... | orbit dlq replay -`

I know about #24 (filters, `--all`) and #92 (JSON output). This is the smaller piece that makes scripting the existing commands fast. I'm happy to send a PR if the maintainers agree on the shape.
author: pkowal

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
+1, this is small and composes with both #24 and #92: however the jobs are selected, replay should take a batch in one process over one connection. Please keep the per-ID output (`replayed <old> -> <new>`) so scripts can still map old IDs to new ones, and exit non-zero if any ID is unknown (see the exit codes in `cli-reference`).

If you want to pick it up, please open a draft PR and follow `contributing` (CLI changes need an entry in the CLI reference and a snapshot test).

comments.author: pkowal
comments.body: Will do, probably in a couple of weeks.

title: ORB-1001 "max number of clients reached" after scaling out workers (no failover involved)
body:
We scaled our worker VMs from 8 to 12 for a seasonal peak. The new workers can't connect, and some of the existing ones start dropping too:

```text
2026-07-04T13:58:02Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 1)
2026-07-04T13:58:04Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 2)
2026-07-04T13:58:08Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: max number of clients reached (attempt 3)
```

There was **no failover**. I checked, because I've read about the 3.1.0 reconnect storm. Redis is a managed instance with `maxclients 400`. We run 12 worker VMs with one `orbit worker --concurrency 32` process each, plus our API servers enqueueing.

How many connections is a worker supposed to hold? It looks like more than one per slot.

Orbit 3.1.0 on Python 3.11.
author: sable-io

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Thanks for ruling out the failover first. This isn't the reconnect storm from #143, it's plain capacity. Each worker process holds roughly `concurrency + 2` connections (one per slot for acks, plus the blocking claim and the heartbeat), so:

```text
before:  8 workers × (32 + 2) = 272  + producers
after:  12 workers × (32 + 2) = 408  + producers  > maxclients 400
```

Options:

- raise `maxclients` (or move to a tier that allows more), with headroom for deploys, when old and new workers overlap for a while;
- or lower `--concurrency`. If the jobs are I/O-bound, 12 × 24 slots may give you the same throughput with 312 worker connections.

The formula is in `broker-redis` ("Sizing and performance"), and `scaling-workers` has the checklist for scaling out.

comments.author: sable-io
comments.body: That's it, the producers add about 50 more. We moved to a tier with `maxclients 2000` and everything connected. Closing, thanks.

title: ORB-1102 WorkerHeartbeatLost reported for every worker on a clean rolling deploy
body:
Every rolling deploy pages our on-call, because we alert on `ORB-1102` and every worker that shuts down cleanly is reported as having lost its heartbeat.

The worker side looks fine. It gets SIGTERM, drains and exits 0:

```text
2026-07-05T09:30:01Z INFO  orbit.worker received SIGTERM, draining (in_flight=3)
2026-07-05T09:30:07Z INFO  orbit.worker drained, released 10 prefetched jobs
2026-07-05T09:30:07Z INFO  orbit.worker stopped worker=w-7f3a exit=0
```

Then about 90 seconds later another worker logs:

```text
2026-07-05T09:31:38Z WARN  orbit.worker ORB-1102 WorkerHeartbeatLost worker=w-7f3a last_seen=2026-07-05T09:30:06Z
```

It's like the shutdown never deregisters the worker, so the heartbeat sweeper thinks it died. Orbit 3.1.0, Python 3.12, Redis broker, Kubernetes with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 330`.

Expected: a worker that drained and exited 0 shouldn't produce ORB-1102.
author: granite-bi

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Confirmed. In 3.1.0 the worker removes its registry entry *after* closing the heartbeat connection, and that write is silently dropped. The sweeper then sees a stale heartbeat. The jobs are fine; no work is lost or duplicated, because they were already released during the drain.

The fix is merged and will be part of **3.1.2**. Until then you can filter on `exit=0` in your alert, or alert on `orbit.workers.online` dropping instead (see `observability-metrics`).

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Shipped in 3.1.2: `WorkerHeartbeatLost` is no longer reported for workers that shut down cleanly. See `changelog`.

title: jobs not running??
body: i enqueue jobs and nothing happens. it worked yesterday. using redis. pls help asap
author: vector-ops

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:

title: Does idempotency_key prevent duplicates on SQS standard queues?
body:
We're on the SQS broker (`sqs://eu-west-1/billing`) with **standard** queues, not FIFO, because we need the throughput. SQS standard queues are at-least-once and occasionally deliver a message twice.

Our job:

```python
@app.job(retries=3, idempotency_key="invoice_id")
def issue_invoice(invoice_id: str, amount_cents: int): ...
```

If SQS delivers the same message twice, does the `idempotency_key` stop the second run? Or does it only dedupe at enqueue time? The `idempotency` page talks about `.enqueue()` results, but I couldn't find anything about redelivery on SQS specifically.

Orbit 3.1.2, Python 3.11.
author: dk-cloud

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Short answer: it dedupes at **enqueue**, not at execution.

The key (`issue_invoice:<invoice_id>`) decides what `.enqueue()` does. A second `.enqueue()` with the same key and the same arguments returns the existing job handle. See the table in `idempotency` ("What happens on enqueue").

It does **not** stop a broker from redelivering a message it already delivered. That's at-least-once delivery, the same thing that happens on any broker when a lease expires (`troubleshooting-duplicates`). On SQS standard queues you can also get the rare native duplicate. So the job body still has to be idempotent. For invoices, check whether the invoice was already issued (or use your payment provider's idempotency header) before you create it.

On FIFO queues Orbit additionally sets `MessageDeduplicationId` to the key, which gives you SQS's 5-minute dedup window on top. See `broker-sqs` ("Idempotency on SQS").

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: We know that section of the SQS docs is thin. It's tracked in #94, and the `faq` entry will point to it once it's expanded.

comments.author: dk-cloud
comments.body: Clear, thanks. We'll add a guard in the job itself.

title: Regression in 3.1.2: per-job backoff ignores [retries] max_delay_seconds again
body:
This looks like #128 again. It was fixed in 3.1.0 and the fix worked for us, but since we upgraded to 3.1.2 the cap stops applying as soon as a job sets `backoff=` itself. The docs say every backoff delay is capped at `max_delay_seconds` (600 by default).

**orbit.toml**

```toml
[retries]
max_attempts = 3
backoff = "exponential"
max_delay_seconds = 600
```

**Job**

```python
@app.job(retries=12, backoff="exponential", timeout="30s")
def push_to_crm(contact_id: str): ...
```

**Worker log (CRM was down for about two hours)**

```text
2026-07-10T02:00:04Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=1 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 1 in 2s
2026-07-10T02:00:07Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=2 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 2 in 3s
...
2026-07-10T02:12:40Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=9 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 9 in 431s
2026-07-10T02:19:51Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=10 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 10 in 877s
2026-07-10T02:34:28Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=11 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 11 in 1702s
2026-07-10T03:02:50Z INFO  orbit.retries push_to_crm attempt=12 failed: HTTPError 503, retry 12 in 3311s
2026-07-10T03:58:01Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted job=01J2KQ7R4D push_to_crm attempts=13 -> dlq
```

Retries 10, 11 and 12 should all have been capped at 600s. Instead the job sat for almost an hour before its last attempt, and the CRM had been back for 40 minutes by then.

If I remove `backoff="exponential"` from the decorator (so it comes from `orbit.toml`), the delays stop at 600s as expected.

Orbit 3.1.2, Python 3.12, Redis broker.
author: juniper-io

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Confirmed, and thanks for the side-by-side. It's a regression, and the third time this symptom has shown up (#23 on 2.8, #128 on 3.0.3). A refactor of how job options are merged in 3.1.2 dropped the inheritance that fixed #128, and the test added for #128 only covered `retries=`, not `backoff=`. When `backoff` is passed to `@app.job`, we build a fresh policy object again and don't copy the global cap into it. That contradicts `retries-and-backoff`, which says the cap applies to every delay.

Workaround for now: drop the per-job `backoff=` if it matches the global value anyway, or lower `retries` so the uncapped delays stay reasonable.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Fix merged: the per-job policy inherits `max_delay_seconds` again, and the test now covers every per-job option. It will go out with 3.2.0. Closing via the PR.

title: ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError on Postgres broker right after password rotation
body:
We rotated the database password for the Orbit user this morning and now every worker fails at startup:

```text
2026-07-11T07:02:44Z ERROR orbit.broker.postgres ORB-1002 BrokerAuthError: password authentication failed for user "orbit_app"
orbit.errors.BrokerAuthError: [ORB-1002] could not authenticate to postgresql://orbit_app@pg-primary.internal.example.com:5432/orbit
```

`psql` with the same password works fine. Here's our config so you can see what we're doing:

```toml
[broker]
url = "postgresql://orbit_app:FAKE/pass@example!1@pg-primary.internal.example.com:5432/orbit?sslmode=require"

[results]
backend = "postgres"
```

and the `.env` that our deploy job loads (in case something here conflicts):

```bash
ORBIT_BROKER_URL=postgresql://orbit_app:old-pass@pg-primary.internal.example.com:5432/orbit
PAYMENTS_API_KEY=sk-test-FAKE-9f3c2a7e41b84d06
SUPPORT_INBOX=billing-alerts@example.com
```

Any idea? This is blocking our billing jobs.

Thanks,
Jane Doe, Platform Team
jane.doe@example.com | 555-0148
1234 Example Avenue, Suite 400, Springfield
author: slate-ripple

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
First, please **rotate that password again** and the `PAYMENTS_API_KEY`. This is a public tracker, and both are now in the issue history. Please also edit them out of the issue (and the contact details in the signature), though edits stay visible in the history, so rotating is the part that matters. `security` has guidance on keeping credentials out of `orbit.toml`.

On the actual problem: the new password contains `/` and `@`. Inside a URL these have to be percent-encoded (`/` → `%2F`, `@` → `%40`, `!` → `%21`). Otherwise everything after the first `@` is parsed as the host, so Orbit is effectively sending a truncated password. `psql` works because you type the password separately.

The `ORBIT_BROKER_URL` line in `.env` isn't the cause. Orbit 3.x ignores `ORBIT_*` variables (see `environment-variables-2x`), but you may as well delete it to avoid confusion.

comments.author: slate-ripple
comments.body: That was it. Percent-encoded it and workers are back. Rotated both secrets as well, sorry about that.

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body: Glad it's sorted. Closing. I'll add a short note about percent-encoding passwords to `broker-postgres`.

title: After upgrading to 3.1.2: ~10 s of ORB-1001 warnings during a failover drill, is that expected?
body:
We skipped 3.1.0 because of the reconnect storm (#143) and went from 3.0.3 straight to 3.1.2 on staging. Before rolling it out to prod we ran a manual failover drill on the staging Redis. It recovered, but the workers still logged a burst of warnings:

```text
2026-07-14T09:40:11Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Connection reset by peer (attempt 1)
2026-07-14T09:40:12Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-staging.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 2)
2026-07-14T09:40:14Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-staging.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 3)
2026-07-14T09:40:19Z WARN  orbit.broker.redis ORB-1001 BrokerConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-staging.internal.example.com:6379. Connection refused. (attempt 4)
2026-07-14T09:40:21Z INFO  orbit.broker.redis connected to redis-staging.internal.example.com:6379 (role=master)
```

About 40 lines like this across 8 workers (concurrency 24), then everything carried on. Two jobs ran a second time a few minutes later.

Is this the expected behaviour now? Our on-call alert fires on any ORB-1001, so I'd like to know what "normal" looks like before we roll this out. Orbit 3.1.2, Python 3.10.
author: copper-kite

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Yes, that's what a healthy failover looks like on 3.1.2. Compare it with the storm in #143, where thousands of lines all said `attempt 1` and landed in the same second. Here each worker process makes one reconnect with jittered, growing delays, and you're connected again about 10 s after the primary went away. `broker-redis` ("Failover and high availability") describes exactly this: a few seconds of ORB-1001, then workers carry on.

The two jobs that ran again are expected too. Their heartbeats were missed during the failover, so their leases ran out and they were redelivered. That's the usual at-least-once caveat (`troubleshooting-duplicates`), so jobs like those need to be idempotent.

For alerting, don't page on a single ORB-1001. Alert when it persists, e.g. `orbit.errors` with `error_code="ORB-1001"` above zero for more than a minute (`observability-metrics`).

comments.author: copper-kite
comments.body: Makes sense, thanks. We changed the alert to "ORB-1001 for more than 60 s" and rolled 3.1.2 out to prod. Closing.

title: Metric for the age of the oldest waiting job per queue
body:
We'd like to alert when work is *stuck* rather than when the queue is merely long.

`orbit.queue.depth` tells us how many jobs are ready, and `orbit.job.queue_wait` tells us how long a job waited, but `queue_wait` is only recorded when a job **starts**. A job that never starts (for example `low` jobs behind a constant stream of `high`) never shows up in that histogram, so the p99 looks great while some jobs have been waiting for an hour.

**Proposal:** a gauge with the age of the oldest ready job, per `queue` and `priority`, reported next to `orbit.queue.depth`. Then the alert is simply "oldest `low` job on `reports` > 30 min".

We're on 3.1.2 and export via OTLP to a Collector, then into Prometheus.
author: hollis-sre

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Agreed that `queue_wait` has survivorship bias. It only sees jobs that made it out of the queue, as you describe. The current metric set is in `observability-metrics`.

An oldest-ready-job gauge is cheap on Redis and Postgres (the claim index is already ordered by `ready_at`). SQS doesn't expose it per priority, so it would probably be the approximate-age attribute there. Labelling as a feature. If someone wants to pick it up, the metric would need a row in the metrics table and a test per broker.

title: ORB-1401 ScheduleParseError on a valid cron step-over-range expression (9-17/2)
body:
This expression is valid in every cron implementation I know (every 2 hours from 09:00 to 17:00 on weekdays), but Orbit rejects it at import time:

```python
app.schedule(refresh_dashboards, cron="0 9-17/2 * * MON-FRI")
```

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/app/tasks.py", line 41, in <module>
    app.schedule(refresh_dashboards, cron="0 9-17/2 * * MON-FRI")
  File "/srv/app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/app.py", line 288, in schedule
    spec = CronSpec.parse(cron)
  File "/srv/app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbit/scheduler/cron.py", line 97, in parse
    raise ScheduleParseError(f"invalid {name} field {raw!r} in cron expression {expr!r}")
orbit.errors.ScheduleParseError: [ORB-1401] invalid hour field '9-17/2' in cron expression '0 9-17/2 * * MON-FRI'
```

`*/2` works, `9-17` works, and the explicit list `0 9,11,13,15,17 * * MON-FRI` works, so I'm using that for now. It's only the `a-b/n` form that fails.

Orbit 3.1.2, Python 3.12.
author: north-pier

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Confirmed. The field parser handles `*/n`, `a-b` and lists, but `a-b/n` falls through to the error branch. `scheduling-cron` says standard 5-field syntax is supported, so this is a bug, not a docs issue.

Your explicit list is the right workaround and gives exactly the same schedule.

comments.author: north-pier
comments.body: Opened a PR with the parser fix and a few table-driven tests for ranges with steps.

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Merged, thanks @north-pier! It will be in the next release. Closing.

title: How long are job results kept, and can I skip storing them for fire-and-forget jobs?
body:
Our Redis memory keeps creeping up and most of it is `orbit:result:*` keys. 95% of our jobs are fire-and-forget (webhooks, cache warmers) and nobody ever reads the result.

1. How long does Orbit keep results by default?
2. Can I turn result storage off for some jobs but not others?
3. Would `[results] backend = "none"` be safe for us? We use idempotency keys on a few jobs, and one Flow.

Orbit 3.1.2, Redis broker + Redis results.
author: velvet-ion

comments.author: mara-k
comments.body:
1. `[results] ttl_days`, default **7**, counted from when the job finishes.
2. Yes, effectively: a job that returns `None` stores no result payload. Only the small status record remains, which also expires with `ttl_days`. Your webhooks and cache warmers probably already return something by accident (a `requests.Response`, a dict), so check that.
3. **No, not in your case.** Idempotency records and Flow run state both live in the result backend. With `backend = "none"`, Flows can't run and idempotency keys stop working.

So: return `None` from the fire-and-forget jobs and consider `ttl_days = 2`. `results-backend` has a sizing formula, and `performance-tuning` ("Result storage") covers the same advice.

comments.author: velvet-ion
comments.body: Returning None from the webhook jobs cut result memory by about 80%. Thanks!

title: error-codes: ORB-1503 entry says "start a new run" but not how to do it safely
body:

2. Purge the run's DLQ entries so nobody replays them into a broken run

title: Long nightly export job runs twice: ORB-1101 LeaseExpired then a second worker picks it up
body:
`export_ledger` runs nightly and takes 7–9 minutes. Every few nights the export file is written twice and the downstream SFTP drop receives two copies. Logs from the two workers:

```text
2026-07-19T01:00:02Z INFO  orbit.worker w-2c91 started job=01J3D8M2QF export_ledger attempt=1
2026-07-19T01:05:02Z WARN  orbit.worker w-2c91 ORB-1101 LeaseExpired job=01J3D8M2QF queue=reports lease_seconds=300
2026-07-19T01:05:03Z INFO  orbit.worker w-88ae started job=01J3D8M2QF export_ledger attempt=2
2026-07-19T01:08:41Z INFO  orbit.worker w-2c91 finished job=01J3D8M2QF export_ledger outcome=succeeded duration=519.2s
2026-07-19T01:13:57Z INFO  orbit.worker w-88ae finished job=01J3D8M2QF export_ledger outcome=succeeded duration=534.0s
```

Config:

```toml
[worker]
concurrency = 4
prefetch = 2
lease_seconds = 300
heartbeat_seconds = 240
```

We raised `heartbeat_seconds` a while ago to reduce Redis writes. Isn't the heartbeat supposed to keep the lease alive? The second run says `attempt=2`, but the first attempt never failed. It finished successfully three minutes later. Orbit 3.1.2, Python 3.11, Redis.
author: amber-shell

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
This is the lease working as designed, but your heartbeat setting leaves almost no margin.

The heartbeat renews the lease every `heartbeat_seconds`. With `lease_seconds = 300` and `heartbeat_seconds = 240`, one heartbeat that's even a minute late (GC pause, a busy event loop, a short Redis hiccup) lets the lease run out. The broker then assumes the worker died and hands the job to someone else. That's the `ORB-1101` you see. A redelivery after lease expiry counts as an attempt (see the table in `retries-and-backoff`), which is why the second worker starts `attempt=2` even though nothing raised.

Fix:

```toml
[worker]
lease_seconds = 900      # longer than your slowest healthy export
heartbeat_seconds = 30   # at most a third of lease_seconds
```

`orbit doctor` warns when `heartbeat_seconds` is more than `lease_seconds / 3`. It's worth running in CI. Heartbeat cost at 30 s is small (see `performance-tuning`, "Heartbeat cost").

Since delivery is at-least-once, also make the export idempotent: write to a temp name and rename, or key the SFTP upload on the ledger date. Background is in `troubleshooting-duplicates` and `leases-and-heartbeats`.

comments.author: amber-shell
comments.body: Missed the doctor warning, it was in our deploy logs all along. Changed both settings and made the upload overwrite by date.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body: Closing as working as designed. Glad the doctor check helped.
