comments.body:
Thank you, this is the most useful report we've had on the Postgres wakeup path. You're right that these are two different things.

**Symptom 1 (night): this is your load balancer.** A connection that only `LISTEN`s sends nothing while there are no notifications, and the 345–356 s pattern looks exactly like a ~350 s TCP idle timeout on the LB. The claim and heartbeat connections stay alive only because they're used. libpq keepalive parameters in the broker URL fix this without any Orbit change:

```toml
[broker]
url = "postgresql://orbit_worker@pg-orbit.internal.example.com:5432/orbit?sslmode=require&keepalives=1&keepalives_idle=60&keepalives_interval=10"
```

**Symptom 2 (load): this is the known issue tracked in #87**, described in `broker-postgres` ("LISTEN/NOTIFY can miss events under load") and the known-issues table in `changelog`. Your logs are the first to show it clearly *without* any reset: the `drained N notifications in one read (queue busy)` lines line up with the windows where polls claim jobs that never got a NOTIFY. No jobs are lost, because the 5 s poll is the safety net, and that's the plateau you see. The poll interval is fixed and not configurable.

comments.author: sable-io
comments.body: Keepalives fixed symptom 1 completely: zero listener resets overnight. Symptom 2 is unchanged in a repeat load test, as you'd expect.

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
On question 3: for a service where the p99 pickup must stay well under a second at 1,000+ jobs/s, Redis is the better fit today. `broker-postgres` puts the comfortable range at a few hundred to about a thousand jobs/s, and `troubleshooting-broker` has the decision notes. Below that load, most teams are fine with an occasional poll-bounded pickup.

Symptom 1 is solved and symptom 2 is #87, so I'm closing this as a duplicate of #87 and linking your logs there. They're the clearest reproduction we have. We'll post on #87 when there's a fix to test.

title: Weighted fair scheduling between priorities (so `low` gets a share)
body:
Feature request: instead of strict priority, let a worker take, say, 70% `high`, 20% `normal`, 10% `low` when all three have ready jobs. Right now `low` gets nothing while there's any `high` work, and in our case there always is during the day.

Orbit 3.2.0. We could probably contribute if the design is agreed.
author: granite-bi

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Thanks! This is the same underlying request as #179 (priority aging). Weighted shares and aging are two ways of solving starvation, and we'd like to discuss them in one place. Please add your proposal and the offer to contribute there.

Today priorities are strict (`concepts-queues-priorities`). The workaround is a separate queue for bulk work consumed by the same workers, since the worker round-robins between queues.

Closing as a duplicate of #179.

title: deployment-kubernetes: explain how to pick terminationGracePeriodSeconds
body:
The "Graceful shutdown" section in `deployment-kubernetes` (added for #56) says to set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to at least your longest expected job, but it doesn't say how that number relates to Orbit's settings. Is "job" the `timeout`? Does the heartbeat or the lease matter?

We set it to exactly our 600 s job timeout and still saw jobs SIGKILLed mid-run during deploys, which then re-ran after the lease expired.

A short section on choosing the value (job timeout, heartbeat, lease) would prevent this. Kubernetes' default of 30 s is almost certainly wrong for most Orbit workers, and "at least the longest job" turns out to be not quite enough.
author: vector-ops

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Agreed, "at least the longest job" was too vague. I've added "Choosing `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`" to `deployment-kubernetes`. The rule is:

```text
terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ longest job timeout + heartbeat_seconds
```

That gives a draining worker time to finish its longest in-flight job and send a final heartbeat, which is why exactly 600 s wasn't enough for your 600 s timeout. It also links to the graceful-shutdown notes in `scaling-workers` and to `troubleshooting-duplicates` for what happens when the pod is killed early.

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Published. Closing, thanks for the report.

title: OIDC redirect loop still happens on 3.2.1
body:
We upgraded the dashboard to 3.2.1 hoping it would fix the login loop, but it still bounces between the dashboard and the IdP until the browser gives up. Logs show the same `ORB-1701 DashboardAuthFailed reason="state mismatch"` lines on every bounce.

Our setup: a cloud L7 load balancer terminates TLS, then ingress-nginx, then the dashboard service. Orbit 3.2.1.
author: kettle-ops

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Right, 3.2.1 doesn't fix this yet. The `changelog` lists it as still open. It's tracked in #209.

Your topology is the tricky one: ingress-nginx sets `X-Forwarded-Proto` itself, but since TLS ends at the load balancer in front of it, it sends `http`. Enable `use-forwarded-headers: "true"` in the ingress-nginx controller ConfigMap so the original `https` is passed through. Details are in `dashboard-auth-oidc` ("Reverse proxies and redirect loops") and `deployment-kubernetes`.

Closing as a duplicate of #209.

comments.author: kettle-ops
comments.body: That was it, use-forwarded-headers fixed it. Thanks.

title: Warn at startup (and in `orbit doctor`) when prefetch > 100 on 3.2.x
body:
Follow-up to #213. The workaround (keep `prefetch` ≤ 100) is documented, but people only find it after they've been OOM-killed. We had a second team hit it this week because their Helm chart sets `prefetch = 256`.

Since the leak is known and the threshold is clear, could the worker log a warning at startup when `prefetch` > 100 on an affected version, and could `orbit doctor` show it as a `[warn]` under `worker`, like the existing `heartbeat_seconds` vs `lease_seconds` check? That would catch it in CI for anyone who runs doctor there.
author: vector-ops

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body: Good idea and cheap to do. The `worker` check in `orbit doctor` already warns about `heartbeat_seconds`, so this fits right in (`cli-reference`). We'd remove the warning again once #213 is fixed. Leaving open as a feature; it may well land before the leak fix itself.

title: Workers OOMKilled every few hours on 3.2.1 (prefetch = 250)
body:
Upgraded to 3.2.1 last night. Workers get OOMKilled every 3–4 hours, and each restart is preceded by `ORB-2101 WorkerOOM rss_mb=3072 limit_mb=3072` in the worker log.

```text
$ kubectl get pods -l app=orbit-worker
NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS        AGE
orbit-worker-6f9c7d9b5d-2xk4p   1/1     Running   3 (41m ago)     11h
orbit-worker-6f9c7d9b5d-8wq7n   1/1     Running   2 (2h14m ago)   11h
orbit-worker-6f9c7d9b5d-tm5rz   1/1     Running   3 (1h02m ago)   11h
```

Last state for each restart is `OOMKilled`. `[worker] concurrency = 12`, `prefetch = 250`. We were on 3.1.2 before and memory was flat.
author: juniper-io

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
This is the open 3.2.x prefetch leak, tracked in #213. It's not fixed in 3.2.1 (see `changelog`, "Still open").

Set `prefetch` to 100 or less and memory will stay flat. If you need the buffering, add worker replicas instead (`scaling-workers`). The details are in `troubleshooting-memory`. Closing as a duplicate of #213.

title: Postgres result backend: expired rows pile up because cleanup can't keep up with throughput
body:
`ttl_days = 3`, but our `orbit_results` table keeps growing and now holds results from **July**:

```text
orbit=> SELECT count(*) FROM orbit_results;
   count
-----------
 182344107
(1 row)

orbit=> SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('orbit_results'));
 pg_size_pretty
----------------
 61 GB
(1 row)
```

`results-backend` says that with Postgres "workers delete expired rows in batches of 1,000 every few minutes". We run ~200 jobs/s, roughly 17 million results a day. At 1,000 rows every few minutes the cleanup removes maybe half a million rows a day, so it can never catch up. Effectively `ttl_days` is ignored for us.

Orbit 3.2.1, PostgreSQL 16, Postgres broker + Postgres results.
author: slate-ripple

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Your arithmetic is right. The fixed batch size was chosen to keep the cleanup from competing with claims, but it doesn't scale with throughput. We'll make it adaptive (keep deleting while there are expired rows, with a time budget per round).

In the meantime:
- return `None` from jobs whose results nobody reads. The row still exists, but it's much smaller (`results-backend`, `performance-tuning`)
- run a batched cleanup of expired rows yourself during quiet hours. Delete in chunks and let autovacuum catch up between chunks, as `broker-postgres` recommends for `orbit.jobs`.

After the backlog is gone, expect a big `VACUUM` before the table shrinks on disk.

comments.author: slate-ripple
comments.body: Thanks. Returning None from our webhook jobs alone should cut the size a lot. Happy to test the adaptive cleanup when there's a branch.

title: Replayed DLQ job goes straight back to the DLQ after one failure (attempt counter not reset)
body:
`cli-reference` says `orbit dlq replay` creates a new job "with the attempt count reset to zero". That's not what we see for a job with a per-job retry policy:

```python
@app.job(retries=8, timeout="2m")
def sync_inventory(warehouse_id: str): ...
```

```text
$ orbit dlq replay j_9c01e2
replayed j_9c01e2 -> j_9c4a77
```

```text
2026-10-25T10:02:13Z WARN  orbit.worker  job j_9c4a77 sync_inventory attempt 9/9 failed: TimeoutError
2026-10-25T10:02:13Z ERROR orbit.retries ORB-1301 RetryExhausted job=j_9c4a77 sync_inventory attempts=9 -> dlq
```

The replayed job starts at attempt 9/9, fails once (the warehouse API was still flaky) and is dead-lettered again immediately. Jobs that use the global `[retries] max_attempts` instead of `retries=` are reset correctly and start at attempt 1.

Orbit 3.2.1, Redis broker.
author: copper-kite

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Reproduced, thanks for narrowing it down to per-job policies. Replay resets the attempt counter on the new job, but a job with its own `retries=` carries its policy state along with the copied headers, and that copy still holds the old attempt number. So the worker sees attempt 9 of 9.

Workaround: replay only after the cause is fixed, which `dead-letter-queue` recommends anyway. For a flaky upstream, you can temporarily deploy the job with a higher `retries=` before replaying.

title: ORB-1502 StepTimeout in a Flow: how do I give one step a longer timeout?
body:
Our `build_index` job is used both on its own (small tenants, a few seconds) and as a step in the `nightly-reindex` Flow, where it processes everything and takes several minutes. In the Flow it fails every night: three attempts in a row end with `ORB-1502 StepTimeout ... timeout=30s`, and then the step lands in the DLQ with `ORB-1301`.

The job is declared with `@app.job(timeout="30s")`, which is right for the standalone case. Can I override the timeout just for the Flow step? And do I need to change `lease_seconds` as well?

Orbit 3.2.1.
author: granite-bi

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Yes, `step()` takes its own `timeout` (and `retries`), which override the job's values for that step only:

```python
reindex = Flow("nightly-reindex", steps=[
    step(collect_tenants),
    step(build_index, after="collect_tenants", timeout="20m", retries=1),
])
```

See the parameter table in `flows-steps-and-state`.

On the lease: step timeout and lease are separate. As long as heartbeats renew the lease (default `heartbeat_seconds = 30`), a 20-minute step is fine with the default `lease_seconds = 300`. If the step blocks the worker (heavy C extensions, tight CPU loops), heartbeats can't be sent and you'd see `ORB-1101` and a duplicate run. The note in `flows-error-handling` ("Step timeouts") covers this.

comments.author: granite-bi
comments.body: Per-step timeout did it, last night's run went through. Thanks again.

title: Dashboard workers view: show heartbeat age for each running job
body:
When a job looks stuck, the first question is "is the worker still alive and heartbeating, or is this a lease about to expire?". Right now the dashboard workers view shows each worker's busy slots and the running job IDs, but not when each job last heartbeated.

Showing "last heartbeat N s ago" next to each running job (and highlighting it when it's more than `lease_seconds / 3`) would make it obvious when a job is about to be redelivered, before ORB-1101 shows up in the logs.

Orbit 3.2.1, Python 3.11.
author: hollis-sre

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body: Nice idea. The heartbeat timestamps are already in the broker for every running job, so the data is there. The threshold you suggest matches the guidance in `leases-and-heartbeats`. Labelled as a feature for the dashboard.

title: Docs: how do idempotency keys and SQS FIFO deduplication interact on replay and on delays?
body:
`broker-sqs` ("Idempotency on SQS") says Orbit sets `MessageDeduplicationId` to the idempotency key on FIFO queues, and then that the section is incomplete. `faq` says the same. We run billing on FIFO queues and the gaps matter to us:

1. If I `orbit dlq replay` a job within 5 minutes of its original send, does SQS drop the replay as a duplicate, since the key and dedup ID are the same?
2. When Orbit re-sends a message (delay hops, retries), does it reuse the same `MessageDeduplicationId`?
3. On **standard** queues, is anything SQS-specific done with the key at all?

A table like the one in `idempotency` ("What happens on enqueue"), but for SQS FIFO vs standard, would answer all of this.
author: dk-cloud

comments.author: ines-v
comments.body:
Thanks, these are exactly the open questions behind the "incomplete" note, and the table format is a good idea. Short answers while the page is being written:

1. Yes, a replay inside SQS's 5-minute deduplication interval can be silently dropped on FIFO queues. Wait at least 5 minutes before replaying (in practice you'll be fixing the cause first anyway).
2. Re-sends currently reuse the same deduplication ID. That's the part we need to document carefully, together with how it interacts with delays.
3. On standard queues SQS has no deduplication, so only Orbit's own idempotency check at enqueue applies (`idempotency`).

The SQS section of `idempotency` is tracked in #94, so I've copied your three questions and the table idea there and I'm closing this as a duplicate.

title: SQS FIFO: delayed job with an idempotency key silently disappears (re-send deduplicated by SQS)
body:
Reminder jobs enqueued with a delay of 1 hour on a FIFO queue never run. There's no error, nothing in the DLQ, and `handle.result()` eventually times out. The same job **without** `idempotency_key`, or with a delay under 15 minutes, works.

```python
@app.job(idempotency_key="appointment_id")
def send_reminder(appointment_id: str): ...

send_reminder.enqueue(appointment_id="ap_4471", delay="1h")
```

Broker: `sqs://eu-central-1/orbit-prod-reminders.fifo`. DEBUG log from the only worker that touched it:

```text
2026-10-29T08:00:02.114Z DEBUG orbit.broker.sqs send job=01JB2QX7MD send_reminder queue=orbit-prod-reminders.fifo delay=3600s mode=hop dedup_id=send_reminder:ap_4471
2026-10-29T08:00:02.981Z DEBUG orbit.broker.sqs received job=01JB2QX7MD not due (3599s remaining), re-sending
2026-10-29T08:00:03.040Z DEBUG orbit.broker.sqs SendMessage ok job=01JB2QX7MD dedup_id=send_reminder:ap_4471
2026-10-29T08:00:03.052Z DEBUG orbit.broker.sqs deleted original message for job=01JB2QX7MD
```

After that, nothing for this job ID, ever. My guess: SQS accepted the re-send (it returns OK for deduplicated messages) but never delivered it, because it has the same `MessageDeduplicationId` as the first send less than a second earlier. Then Orbit deleted the original, and the job is gone.

We lost ~1,200 appointment reminders before we noticed. Orbit 3.2.1, Python 3.12.
author: north-pier

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Thank you for the precise log. Your reading is correct, and this is a real job-loss bug.

FIFO queues don't support per-message `DelaySeconds`, so on FIFO Orbit falls back to hopping from the start, re-sending until the job is due. Every re-send reuses the idempotency key as `MessageDeduplicationId`. A re-send inside SQS's 5-minute interval is accepted but never delivered, and since we delete the original after a "successful" send, the job is lost. Standard queues and short delays don't hop this way, which is why they work.

Immediate workarounds (pick one):
- drop `idempotency_key` from delayed jobs on FIFO queues and dedupe inside the job
- use a standard queue for delayed work
- for reminders, use a cron schedule plus a dispatcher job instead of long delays (`scheduling-cron`, `scheduling-delays`)

Fix direction: give hops their own deduplication ID, derived from the key plus the hop number. Labelled S2; the documentation side is tracked in #237.

comments.author: north-pier
comments.body: Moved delayed reminders to a standard queue for now. Happy to test a fix.

title: SQS: do I need to set the queue's visibility timeout to match lease_seconds?
body:
Setting up the SQS broker with Terraform. Our queues have the AWS default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. Some jobs take ~10 minutes.

Do I need to set each queue's visibility timeout to `lease_seconds` (300) or higher, or does Orbit handle that? I couldn't tell from `broker-sqs` whether the queue setting matters.

Orbit 3.2.1.
author: velvet-ion

comments.author: sam-okafor
comments.body:
Orbit handles it. On receive it sets the message's visibility timeout to `lease_seconds`, and each heartbeat extends it with `ChangeMessageVisibility` every `heartbeat_seconds` (mapping table in `broker-sqs`). The queue-level default only matters for messages received by something other than Orbit.

Two things to check:
- the IAM policy must allow `sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility` (the example policy in `broker-sqs` includes it), or heartbeats fail and 10-minute jobs get redelivered (`ORB-1101`)
- SQS caps visibility at 12 hours, so a single lease can't be longer than that

Background on leases vs visibility timeouts is in `leases-and-heartbeats` and `glossary`.

comments.author: velvet-ion
comments.body: Perfect, our policy was missing ChangeMessageVisibility. Thanks!

title: Nightly 01:30 job ran twice last night (US DST fall back), ORB-1402 in logs: expected?
body:
Our nightly invoice run is scheduled with:

```python
app.schedule(send_invoices_nightly, cron="30 1 * * *")
```

Workers run in `America/Chicago`. Last night the clocks went back at 02:00 CDT and the job ran **twice**, an hour apart:

```text
2026-11-01T01:30:00-05:00 INFO  orbit.scheduler fired send_invoices_nightly (cron="30 1 * * *")
2026-11-01T01:30:00-06:00 WARN  orbit.scheduler [ORB-1402] ScheduleDrift: send_invoices_nightly due 2026-11-01T01:30:00-05:00
fired 2026-11-01T01:30:00-06:00 (local time repeated by DST transition)
2026-11-01T01:30:00-06:00 INFO  orbit.scheduler fired send_invoices_nightly (cron="30 1 * * *")
```

Luckily the invoice job checks whether today's batch was already sent, so customers didn't get two invoices. But I'd like to know if this is expected and what the recommended setup is. Orbit 3.2.1.
author: amber-shell

comments.author: devon-li
comments.body:
Expected, unfortunately. This is the long-standing DST limitation tracked in #59, and it's in the DST table in `scheduling-cron`. Cron expressions are evaluated in the local time zone of the worker holding the scheduler lock. On a fall-back night 01:00–01:59 happens twice, so `30 1 * * *` can fire twice and log ORB-1402.

Recommended setup:
1. Run all workers in UTC (`TZ=UTC`) and write the expression in UTC. 01:30 in Chicago is `30 7 * * *` in winter and `30 6 * * *` in summer, so pick one and accept the one-hour shift twice a year.
2. Keep the "already sent today?" check. Better still, take the billing date as an argument and use it as the idempotency key from a small dispatcher job (`idempotency`, "Scheduled jobs"). A double fire is then a no-op by construction.

Closing as a duplicate of #59, which is where any change to DST behaviour will be announced.

comments.author: amber-shell
comments.body: Thanks, moving the workers to UTC and adding the dispatcher pattern. Subscribed to #59.
